text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 6 2 BACTERIAL STRUCTURE, CLASSIFICATION & GROWTH ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Classify clinically important bacteria according to their morphology, Gram-stain characteristics, and oxygen requirements, using findings from clinical and laboratory contexts. 2. Differentiate the structural features of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and explain how these differences influence their susceptibility to antibiotics. 3. Analyse the contribution of major bacterial structures—including the cell wall, capsule, pili, flagella, plasmids, cell membrane, and endospores—to bacterial survival, colonization, virulence, antimicrobial resistance, and persistence in clinical settings. 4. Interpret bacterial growth-curve data and predict how the different growth phases and environmental conditions may influence bacterial multiplication and the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapy. Bacterial size and shape The small size (0.5 – 5 µm) and nearly colorless nature of bacteria require the use of stains (Gram stain) for visualization with a light microscope.

Interpret bacterial growth-curve data and predict how the different growth phases and environmental conditions may influence bacterial multiplication and the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapy. Bacterial size and shape The small size (0.5 – 5 µm) and nearly colorless nature of bacteria require the use of stains (Gram stain) for visualization with a light microscope. Hence, bacteria are generally referred to Gram positive (violet) and Gram negative (red). The major morphologic forms are spheres, rods, bent or curved rods, and spirals. Spherical or oval bacteria are called cocci and are typically arranged in clusters or chains. Rods are called bacilli and may be straight or curved. Bacilli that are small and pleomorphic to the point of resembling cocci are often called coccobacilli. Structure of Bacteria The major structures of the bacterial cell consist of the multilayered envelope and its appendages and the interior core consisting of the nucleoid (or nuclear body) and the cytoplasm. Figure 1: Structure of bacteria 1. Envelope and appendages A. Cell Wall A rigid cell wall surrounds all bacterial cells except bacteria lacking cell walls such as the mycoplasmas.

Figure 1: Structure of bacteria 1. Envelope and appendages A. Cell Wall A rigid cell wall surrounds all bacterial cells except bacteria lacking cell walls such as the mycoplasmas. The structure and function of the bacterial wall is a hallmark of the prokaryotes; it is absent in human cell. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 6 The cell wall (1) protects the cell from mechanical disruption and from bursting caused by the internal pressure of the cell. (2) It also provides a barrier against certain toxic chemical and biologic agents. (3) Its form is responsible for the shape of the cell. (4) Site of action of beta lactams (penicillin binding proteins; PBP) (5) Contains receptor for phages. The structure, chemical composition, and thickness of the cell wall differ in gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. The peptidoglycan layer is much thicker in Gram-positive than in Gram-negative bacteria. Gram-positive bacteria also have teichoic acid that protrude outside the peptidoglycan, whereas gram-negative bacteria do not.

The peptidoglycan layer is much thicker in Gram-positive than in Gram-negative bacteria. Gram-positive bacteria also have teichoic acid that protrude outside the peptidoglycan, whereas gram-negative bacteria do not. Besides the major wall components—peptidoglycan and teichoic acids—gram-positive walls usually have lesser amounts of other molecules characteristic of their species. Some are polysaccharides, such as the group-specific antigens of streptococci; others are proteins, such as the M protein of group A streptococci. In contrast, Gram-negative bacteria have a complex outer membrane layer consisting of outer leaflet of lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), lipoprotein, and inner leaflet of phospholipid. Special structural proteins, called porins, form pores through the outer membrane that make it possible for nutrients to diffuse through it and into the periplasm. Lying between the outer-membrane layer and the cytoplasmic membrane in Gram-negative bacteria is the periplasmic space, which is the site, in some species, of enzymes called β-lactamases that degrade penicillins and other β-lactam drugs.

Lying between the outer-membrane layer and the cytoplasmic membrane in Gram-negative bacteria is the periplasmic space, which is the site, in some species, of enzymes called β-lactamases that degrade penicillins and other β-lactam drugs. Peptidoglycan Peptidoglycan consists of a linear glycan chain of two alternating sugars, N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM). Adjacent glycan chains are cross-linked into sheets by peptide amino acids side chains. Most enzymes found in mammalian hosts and other biologic systems do not degrade peptidoglycan; one important exception is lysozyme, the hydrolase in tears and other secretions. Treatment of a gram-positive cell with penicillin (which blocks formation of the peptide cross-links) destroys the peptidoglycan, and bacteria is lysed, but If the cell is protected from lysis by suspension in a medium isotonic with the cell interior, the cell becomes round and forms a sphere called a protoplast surrounded by cell membrane. A B Figure 2. A. Peptidoglycan structure. B. Protoplast Teichoic acid These compounds are polymers of either glycerol phosphate or ribitol phosphate.

A B Figure 2. A. Peptidoglycan structure. B. Protoplast Teichoic acid These compounds are polymers of either glycerol phosphate or ribitol phosphate. A type of teichoic acid called lipoteichoic acid and appears to play a role in anchoring the wall to the cell membrane and as an epithelial cell adhesin. It is also the major antigen of Gram-positive bacteria. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 6 Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) LPS consists of: (1) lipid A (the endotoxin), (2) a core polysaccharide, and (3) O antigen polysaccharide side chains (the major surface antigen of gram-negative bacteria). LPS of the outer membrane of the cell wall of gram-negative bacteria is endotoxin. It is responsible for many of the features of disease, such as fever and shock (especially hypotension), caused by these organisms. B.

LPS of the outer membrane of the cell wall of gram-negative bacteria is endotoxin. It is responsible for many of the features of disease, such as fever and shock (especially hypotension), caused by these organisms. B. Cell membrane The cell (plasma) membrane of bacteria is similar to the familiar bi-leaflet membrane of most cells, containing phospholipids. However, bacterial cell membrane does not contain sterols (except mycoplasmas). The cell membrane: (1) plays a role in the segregation of daughter chromosomes at cell division. (2) is the site of synthesis of DNA, cell wall polymers. (3) It contains the entire electron transport system of the cell (and, hence, is functionally analogous to the mitochondria of eukaryotes). (4) It contains receptor proteins that function in chemotaxis. (5) it is a permeability barrier and contains proteins involved in the selective and active transport of solutes. (6) It is also involved in secretion of proteins including exotoxins and hydrolytic enzymes involved in the pathogenesis of disease.

(5) it is a permeability barrier and contains proteins involved in the selective and active transport of solutes. (6) It is also involved in secretion of proteins including exotoxins and hydrolytic enzymes involved in the pathogenesis of disease. The bacterial cell membrane is therefore the functional equivalent of most of the organelles of the eukaryotic cell and is vital to the growth and maintenance of the cell. C. Capsule Many bacterial cells surround themselves with some kind of hydrophilic gel. If the material forms a reasonably discrete layer, it is called a capsule; if it is amorphous, it is referred to as a slime layer. Most capsules are polysaccharides; a few are simple polypeptides. Capsules provide some general protection for bacteria, but their major function in pathogenic bacteria is protection from the immune system (antiphagocytic). Capsular polysaccharides can also form the basis of serotyping and vaccine targets. D. Pili (or Fimbriae) Hair-like projections found on the surface of cells of many Gram-positive and Gram-negative species. There are two general classes, common pili and sex pili.

text: D. Pili (or Fimbriae) Hair-like projections found on the surface of cells of many Gram-positive and Gram-negative species. There are two general classes, common pili and sex pili. Common pili are adhesins, which are responsible for the ability of bacteria to colonize surfaces and cells. The sex pilus is involved in the exchange of genetic material between some Gram-negative bacteria (conjugation). E. Flagella Flagella are organelles of motility found in many species of bacteria, both Gram- positive and Gram-negative. They may be distributed around the cell, at one pole or at both ends of the cell. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 6 2. Core A. Cytoplasm It is densely packed with ribosomes, which are much more abundant than in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells. This is a reflection of the higher growth rate of bacteria. The overall subunit structure of the 70 S bacterial ribosome resembles that of eukaryotic ribosomes, but is smaller and differs sufficiently in function that a very large number of antimicrobial agents have the prokaryotic ribosome as their target. text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 6 3 PATHOGENESIS OF BACTERIAL INFECTION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Interpret clinical findings to distinguish bacterial colonization from infection and relate them to pathogenicity and virulence. 2. Analyze the sequential mechanisms by which bacteria enter the host, adhere to target cells, invade tissues, and evade host defenses. 3. Predict the contribution of specific bacterial virulence mechanisms to the development and severity of clinical disease. 4. Compare the mechanisms and clinical consequences of bacterial exotoxins and endotoxin-mediated injury. 1. Important definitions • Adherence (adhesion, attachment): The process by which bacteria stick to the surfaces of host cells. It is a major initial step in the infection process. • Colonization: colonization is the presence of multiplying bacteria on a body surface (like on the skin, mouth, intestines or airway) without causing disease in the person. • Infection: Invasion & multiplication of an infectious agent within the body to cause disease.

• Colonization: colonization is the presence of multiplying bacteria on a body surface (like on the skin, mouth, intestines or airway) without causing disease in the person. • Infection: Invasion & multiplication of an infectious agent within the body to cause disease. • Pathogenicity: The ability of any bacterial species to cause disease in a susceptible human host. • Pathogen: A bacterial species able to cause such disease when presented with favorable circumstances (for the organism). • Opportunistic pathogen: An agent capable of causing disease only when the host resistance is impaired (ie, when the patient is “immunocompromised”). • Virulence: A term which presumes pathogenicity, but allows expression of degrees from low to extremely high, for example: • Low virulence—Streptococcus salivarius is universally present in the oropharyngeal flora of humans. On its own, it seems incapable of disease production, but if during a transient bacteremia it lands on a damaged heart valve, it can stick and cause infective endocarditis.

• Virulence: A term which presumes pathogenicity, but allows expression of degrees from low to extremely high, for example: • Low virulence—Streptococcus salivarius is universally present in the oropharyngeal flora of humans. On its own, it seems incapable of disease production, but if during a transient bacteremia it lands on a damaged heart valve, it can stick and cause infective endocarditis. • Moderate virulence—Escherichia coli is universally found in the colon, but if displacement to other sites such as adjacent tissues or the urinary bladder regularly causes acute infection. • High virulence—Bordetella pertussis, the cause of whooping cough, is not found in the resident flora, but if encountered it is highly infectious and causes disease in almost every nonimmune person it contacts. • Extremely high virulence—Yersinia pestis, the cause of plague, is also highly infectious, but in addition leads to death in a few days in over 70% of cases. Bacterial pathogenesis is influenced by both microbial virulence factors and host factors.

• Extremely high virulence—Yersinia pestis, the cause of plague, is also highly infectious, but in addition leads to death in a few days in over 70% of cases. Bacterial pathogenesis is influenced by both microbial virulence factors and host factors. The same organism may cause asymptomatic colonization in one host but invasive disease in another, depending on inoculum, portal of entry, host immunity, underlying disease, and the local microbiome. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 6 Attributes of bacterial pathogenicity Whether a microbe is a primary or opportunistic pathogen, it must be able to enter a host; find a unique niche; avoid, circumvent, or subvert normal host defenses; multiply; and injure the host. For long-term success as a pathogen, it must also establish itself in the host or somewhere else long enough to eventually be transmitted to a new susceptible host. 1. Entry Each of the portals in the body that communicates with the outside world becomes a potential site of microbial entry. Human have various protective mechanisms to prevent microbial entry. a.

Entry Each of the portals in the body that communicates with the outside world becomes a potential site of microbial entry. Human have various protective mechanisms to prevent microbial entry. a. A simple, though relatively efficient mechanical barrier to microbial invasion is provided by the epithelial borders of the internal and external body surfaces. Of these, the skin is the most formidable with its tough keratinized superficial layer. Organisms can gain access to the underlying tissues only by breaks or by way of hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands that traverse the stratified layers. Bacteria have no known mechanism for passing the unbroken skin. b. For the internal surfaces a viscous mucin secreted by goblet cells protects the epithelium lining of the respiratory tract, the gastrointestinal tract, and the urogenital system. Microorganisms become trapped in this thick network of protein and polysaccharide and may be swept away before they reach the epithelial cell surface. c. Secretory IgA (sIgA) secreted into the mucus and other secreted antimicrobials such as lysozyme and lactoferrin aid this cleansing process.

Microorganisms become trapped in this thick network of protein and polysaccharide and may be swept away before they reach the epithelial cell surface. c. Secretory IgA (sIgA) secreted into the mucus and other secreted antimicrobials such as lysozyme and lactoferrin aid this cleansing process. Some bacteria excrete an enzyme sIgA protease, which cleaves human sIgA1. (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae). This enzyme may play an important role in establishing microbial species at the mucosal surface. d. The epithelium of the intestinal tract below the esophagus is a less efficient mechanical barrier than the skin, but there are other effective defense mechanisms. The high level of hydrochloric acid and gastric enzymes in the normal stomach kill many ingested bacteria. Other bacteria are susceptible to pancreatic digestive enzymes or to bile salts. How efficiently bacterial pathogens navigate all these barriers before their initial encounter with their target cell type is in some ways measured by their infecting dose. How many organisms must be given to a host to ensure infection in some proportion of the individuals?

How efficiently bacterial pathogens navigate all these barriers before their initial encounter with their target cell type is in some ways measured by their infecting dose. How many organisms must be given to a host to ensure infection in some proportion of the individuals? In general, pathogens that have environmental or animal reservoirs can overwhelm innate defenses with large numbers. Pathogens with no reservoir or amplification mechanism must be transmitted human-to-human and thus require the lowest infecting doses. Without this advantage, these pathogens would eventually die out in the population. 2. Adherence The first major interaction between a pathogenic microorganism and its host entails attachment to a eukaryotic cell surface. In its simplest form, adherence requires the participation of two factors: an adhesin on the invading microbe and a receptor on the host cell. The adhesin must be exposed on the bacterial surface either alone or in association with appendages like pili. In gram-negative bacteria, the outer membrane is a major site for adhesins. Most adhesins are proteins, but carbohydrates and teichoic acids may also be involved.

The adhesin must be exposed on the bacterial surface either alone or in association with appendages like pili. In gram-negative bacteria, the outer membrane is a major site for adhesins. Most adhesins are proteins, but carbohydrates and teichoic acids may also be involved. Two of the most common receptors, mannose and fibronectin, are widely present on human epithelial cell surfaces. Many bacteria have NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 6 more than one mechanism of host cell attachment. Biofilms may also act as an adherence mechanism by binding to catheters, prosthetic devices, or mucosal surfaces. A. B. Figure 1. A. Bacterial attachment. B. Bacterial invasion 3. Invasion A few bacteria (as Chlamydia), like viruses, are obligate intracellular pathogens. Other bacteria are facultative intracellular pathogens and can grow as free-living cells in the environment as well as within host cells. Generally, invasive organisms adhere to host cells by one or more adhesins but use a class of molecules, called invasins, which interact with integrins or other families of cell adhesion molecules.

Generally, invasive organisms adhere to host cells by one or more adhesins but use a class of molecules, called invasins, which interact with integrins or other families of cell adhesion molecules. The integrins in turn interact with elements of the cell cytoskeleton stimulating modifications which end in uptake of the bacterial cell. Invasive bacteria enter cells initially within a membrane-bound, host-vesicular structure but then follow one of two pathways; 1) Some bacteria (Listeria, Shigella) enzymatically lyse the phagosome membrane and escape to the nutrient-rich host cell cytoplasm. These bacteria may continue to multiply there, infect adjacent cells, or move through the cell to the submucosa. 2) Other invasive pathogenic species (Salmonella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) remain in the phagosome and replicate even in phagocytes by preventing phagosome–lysosome fusion or, if fused, blocking acidification to the optimum pH for digestive enzyme activity. 4. Evading the immune system The host immune system evolved in large part because of the selective pressure of microbial attack.

text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 4 BACTERIAL GENETICS ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Identify the major forms of bacterial genetic material and relate their genetic organization to clinically important bacterial characteristics. 2. Analyze how mutations, recombination, and transposable elements can generate phenotypic changes relevant to bacterial survival and antimicrobial resistance. 3. Differentiate transformation, transduction, and conjugation according to their mechanisms and clinical consequences for horizontal gene transfer. 4. Evaluate the applications of recombinant DNA technology in medicine, including the role of vectors and DNA-modifying enzymes. Types of Bacterial DNA 1. Chromosome Single circular double stranded supercoiled DNA molecule. 2. Plasmids Extrachromosomal, double-stranded, circular DNA molecules that are capable of replicating independently of the bacterial chromosome. Although plasmids are usually extrachromosomal, they can be integrated into the bacterial chromosome. Plasmids occur in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.

Plasmids Extrachromosomal, double-stranded, circular DNA molecules that are capable of replicating independently of the bacterial chromosome. Although plasmids are usually extrachromosomal, they can be integrated into the bacterial chromosome. Plasmids occur in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Types of plasmids: (1) Transmissible plasmids (Conjugative plasmids) e.g. F plasmids can be transferred from cell to cell by conjugation. they contain genes responsible for synthesis of the sex pilus and for the enzymes required for transfer. (2) Nontransmissible (Non conjugative) plasmids do not contain the transfer genes. Plasmids carry the genes for the following functions:(1) Antibiotic resistance, (e.g. R plasmids) which is mediated by a variety of enzymes, such as the beta-lactamases. (2) Exotoxins, such as the exfoliative toxin of S. aureus and tetanus toxin of Clostridium tetani. (3) Pili (fimbriae), which mediate the adherence of bacteria to epithelial cells. 3. Transposable elements Transposons are pieces of DNA that move readily from one site to another either within or between the DNAs of bacteria, plasmids, and bacteriophages. They are nicknamed “jumping genes.

Transposable elements Transposons are pieces of DNA that move readily from one site to another either within or between the DNAs of bacteria, plasmids, and bacteriophages. They are nicknamed “jumping genes.” In contrast to plasmids, transposons are not capable of independent replication; they replicate as part of the DNA in which they are integrated. Transposons can code for drug- resistant enzymes, toxins, or a variety of metabolic enzymes and can either cause mutations in the gene into which they insert or alter the expression of nearby genes. Genetic change Bacteria use mutation and recombination for genomic change, as do eukaryotic cells. In addition, they have powerful mechanisms for exchange of genes between cells that do not even have to be closely related. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 1. Mutation The spontaneous development of mutations is a major factor in the evolution of bacteria. Mutations occur in nature at a low frequency (one mutation in every million cells for any one gene), but the large size of microbial populations ensures the presence of many mutants.

Mutations occur in nature at a low frequency (one mutation in every million cells for any one gene), but the large size of microbial populations ensures the presence of many mutants. Because bacteria are haploid, the consequences of a mutation, are immediately evident in the mutant cell. Because the generation time of bacteria is short, it does not take many hours for a mutant cell that has arisen by chance to grow to the dominant cell type if the mutation gives it a survival advantage. 2. Recombination Recombination is the process in which nucleic acid molecules from different sources are combined or rearranged to produce a new nucleotide sequence. The source of recombinant DNA may be another part of the same chromosome or from outside the cell from one of the genetic transfer mechanisms described later. There are two types of recombination: homologous and nonhomologous. a. Homologous recombination occurs between closely related DNA sequences and generally substitutes one sequence for another. The process requires a set of enzymes produced by the rec genes. b.

Homologous recombination occurs between closely related DNA sequences and generally substitutes one sequence for another. The process requires a set of enzymes produced by the rec genes. b. Site-specific recombination occurs between dissimilar DNA sequences and generally produces insertions or deletions or both. This process usually requires specialized recombination enzymes, such as those produced by many transposons and lysogenic bacteriophages. 3. Genetic transfer within bacterial cell Transposition Transposition involves transposable elements that are genetic units capable of mediating their own transfer from one chromosome to another, from one location to another on the same chromosome, or between chromosome and plasmid within the same bacterial cell. This transposition relies on their ability to synthesize their own site-specific recombination enzymes, called transposases. Transposons (1) when inserted in a new site they cause insertional mutation. (2) Sometimes they insert into genes and inactivate gene that encodes an essential protein, then the cell dies.

Mechanisms of antibiotic resistance Non-genetic causes of antibiotic resistance There are several nongenetic reasons for the failure of drugs to inhibit the growth of bacteria: (1) Bacteria can be walled off within an abscess cavity that the drug cannot penetrate effectively. Surgical drainage is therefore a necessary adjunct to chemotherapy. (2) Bacteria can be in a resting state (i.e., not growing); they are therefore insensitive to cell wall inhibitors such as penicillins and cephalosporins. (3) Under certain circumstances, organisms that would ordinarily be killed by penicillin can lose their cell walls, survive as protoplasts, and be insensitive to cell wall–active drugs. Later, if such organisms resynthesize their cell walls, they are fully susceptible to these drugs. (4) The presence of foreign bodies makes successful antibiotic treatment more difficult.

Later, if such organisms resynthesize their cell walls, they are fully susceptible to these drugs. (4) The presence of foreign bodies makes successful antibiotic treatment more difficult. This applies to foreign bodies such as surgical implants and catheters as well as materials that enter the body at the time of penetrating injuries, such as splinters. (5) Several artifacts can make it appear that the organisms are resistant (e.g., administration of the wrong drug or the wrong dose or failure of the drug to reach the appropriate site in the body). A good example of the latter is the poor penetration into spinal fluid by several early-generation cephalosporins. Viruses are the smallest replicating intracellular microorganisms that are comprised of sets of genes either DNA (DNA viruses) or RNA (RNA viruses) packaged in a capsid (protein shell) or in a capsid and an outer lipid bilayer envelope. The resulting complete virus particle is called a virion.

Viruses are the smallest replicating intracellular microorganisms that are comprised of sets of genes either DNA (DNA viruses) or RNA (RNA viruses) packaged in a capsid (protein shell) or in a capsid and an outer lipid bilayer envelope. The resulting complete virus particle is called a virion. Viruses have an obligate requirement for intracellular growth and a heavy dependence on host cell structural and metabolic components. Therefore, viruses are also referred to as obligate intracellular parasites. Viruses do not have a nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, or other cell organelles. Structure of viruses Viruses are approximately 20-400 nm in diameter. The basic structure of all viruses places the nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA) on the inside of a protein shell called a capsid. Some human viruses are further packaged into a lipid membrane, or envelope, which is usually acquired from the plasma or cytoplasmic membrane of the infected cell during release from the cell.

Some human viruses are further packaged into a lipid membrane, or envelope, which is usually acquired from the plasma or cytoplasmic membrane of the infected cell during release from the cell. The genomes of enveloped viruses form a protein complex and a structure called a nucleocapsid, which is often surrounded by a matrix protein that serves as a bridge between the nucleocapsid and the inside of the envelope. Viruses that are not enveloped have a defined external capsid and are referred to as naked viruses. Protein or glycoprotein structures called spikes, which often protrude from the surface of virus particles, are involved in the initial contact with receptor on host cells. The simplest viral structures that can be built stepwise are symmetric and include helical and icosahedral (cubic) structures. Viral genomes Viral genomes can be made of either RNA or DNA and also can be either single-stranded or double-stranded. The RNA viruses can be either positive sense (+) (same polarity of mRNA) or negative sense (–) (complementary to or antisense of mRNA), double- stranded (one strand + and the second strand –) or ambisense (both + and – polarity on the same strand).

The RNA viruses can be either positive sense (+) (same polarity of mRNA) or negative sense (–) (complementary to or antisense of mRNA), double- stranded (one strand + and the second strand –) or ambisense (both + and – polarity on the same strand). Although the RNA genomes of most viruses are linear, some RNA viruses may also have segmented genomes (several segments or pieces of RNA), with each segment responsible for encoding a protein. The DNA genome of viruses can be both linear and circular genomes. Most viruses contain a single copy of their genome, except that retroviruses (e.g HIV) carry two identical copies of its genome and are, therefore, diploid. The capsids of all viruses are composed of many copies of one or, at most, several different kinds of protein subunits. The presence of many identical protein subunits in viral capsids or the existence of many identical spikes in the membrane of enveloped viruses has important implications for adsorption, hemagglutination, and recognition of viruses by neutralizing antibodies. The protein shell forming the capsid or the nucleocapsid assumes one of two basic shapes: helical or icosahedral. Viral envelope Many human viruses have an outer lipid bilayer membrane that is derived from host plasma membrane. The viral envelope lipid layer membrane contains virus-encoded glycoproteins called “spikes” or “peplomers” or “viral envelope proteins.” The envelope spikes bind to the receptor on the host cells, help the virus envelope membrane fuse with the cellular membrane of the host cells, and act as principal antigens against which the host mounts immune response for the recognition of the virus.

Enveloped viruses are more sensitive to detergents, solvents, ethanol, ether, and heat compared with nonenveloped (naked capsid) viruses whose outer coat is capsid protein. Both envelope glycoproteins, and naked capsid viruses’ spikes become antigens after infection and the host mounts both cell-mediated and humoral immune responses for the elimination of virus-infected cells and cell-free virus, respectively. These antigens also determine the viral serotypes that are based on antigenic variation and are type-specific such as poliovirus serotypes 1, 2, and 3. Enveloped viruses are much more heat labile, rapidly at 37°C. Viral infectivity is generally destroyed by heating at 50–60°C for 30 minutes, although there are some exceptions (eg, hepatitis B virus). Viruses can be preserved by storage at freezing temperatures, pH Viruses are usually stable between pH values of 5 – 9. Some viruses (eg, enteroviruses) are resistant to acidic conditions. All viruses are destroyed by alkaline conditions. Radiation Ultraviolet, x-ray inactivate viruses. Formaldehyde It destroys viral infectivity by reacting with nucleic acid. Viruses with single-stranded genomes are inactivated much more readily than those with double-stranded genomes. Formaldehyde has minimal adverse effects on the antigenicity of proteins and therefore has been used in the production of inactivated viral vaccines. Formaldehyde has minimal adverse effects on the antigenicity of proteins and therefore has been used in the production of inactivated viral vaccines. Chlorine Larger concentrations of chlorine are required to destroy viruses than to kill bacteria, especially in the presence of extraneous proteins. For example, the chlorine treatment of stools adequate to inactivate typhoid bacilli is inadequate to destroy poliomyelitis virus present in feces. Quaternary ammonium compounds and organic iodine compounds not effective against viruses Alcohol Alcohols, such as isopropanol and ethanol, are relatively ineffective against certain viruses, especially picornaviruses. Classification of viruses The International Committee for Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) considered various properties, including virions, genome, proteins, envelope, replication, and physical and biologic properties. Based on these properties, virus families are designated with the suffix, -viridae (as in Herpesviridae), virus subfamilies with suffix virinae (Herpesvirinae), virus genera with suffix virus (Herpesvirus), and virus species designated by a virus type (herpes simplex virus 1). NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 8 VIRAL REPLICATION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Outline the major stages of the viral replication cycle and predict the consequence of disruption at each stage. 2. Analyse how differences in viral genome type and cellular machinery determine the strategy of DNA and RNA viral replication. 3. Interpret how viral attachment, entry, replication, assembly, and release contribute to viral pathogenesis and potential immune protection. 4. Differentiate lytic and lysogenic bacteriophage replication and explain their clinical consequences, including lysogenic conversion. Virus replication depends on virus–host cell interaction and the type of cells it infects—whether permissive or nonpermissive cells. 1) Permissive cells are those that permit production of progeny virus particles and/or viral transformation. 2) Nonpermissive cells do not allow virus replication, but may allow virus transformation. Some viruses enter cells that do not support virus replication, but some early viral proteins cause cell death; this infection is termed abortive infection.

2) Nonpermissive cells do not allow virus replication, but may allow virus transformation. Some viruses enter cells that do not support virus replication, but some early viral proteins cause cell death; this infection is termed abortive infection. Viral replication cycle Virus replication cycle typically consists of six discrete phases: (1) adsorption or attachment to the host cell, (2) penetration or entry, and uncoating to release the genome, (3) synthetic or virion component production, (4) assembly, and (5) release from the cell. The eclipse phase in virus replication is the time interval between when a virus infects a host cell and when the first new, infectious virus particles (virions) are assembled inside the cell. Figure 1. Viral replication cycle 1. Adsorption or attachment The first step in every viral infection is the attachment or adsorption of the infecting virus particle to the surface of the host cell. A prerequisite for this interaction is a collision between the virion and the cell.

Adsorption or attachment The first step in every viral infection is the attachment or adsorption of the infecting virus particle to the surface of the host cell. A prerequisite for this interaction is a collision between the virion and the cell. Viruses do not have any capacity for locomotion and, therefore, the collision event is simply a random process determined by diffusion and by the concentrations of both the virions and the cells. It involves interaction between virion attachment proteins (VAP) or spikes and cell receptors. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 For some viruses, two different surface molecules, receptor and coreceptor, are involved in adsorption (ex; HIV). A particular kind of virus is capable of infecting only a limited spectrum of cell types called its host range. In many cases, human viruses infect only a particular subset of the cells found in their host organism. This kind of tissue tropism is clearly an important determinant of viral pathogenesis.

In many cases, human viruses infect only a particular subset of the cells found in their host organism. This kind of tissue tropism is clearly an important determinant of viral pathogenesis. In most cases studied, the specific host range of a virus and its associated tissue tropism are determined at the level of the binding between the cell receptors and virion attachment proteins. When a virus particle has penetrated to the inside of a cell, it is hidden from the host immune system. Thus, if protection from a virus infection is to be accomplished at the level of antibody binding to the virions, it must occur before adsorption and prevent the virus from attaching to and penetrating the cell. Thus, most neutralizing antibodies—whether elicited as a result of natural infection or vaccination— are specific for virion attachment proteins. 2. Penetration, Entry and uncoating After entry, uncoating releases the viral genome or replication-competent nucleocapsid. Uncoating step (capsid disassembly from the viral genome) may be simultaneous with entry or may occur in a series of steps. There are two basic mechanisms for the entry of an enveloped virus into the cell.

Uncoating step (capsid disassembly from the viral genome) may be simultaneous with entry or may occur in a series of steps. There are two basic mechanisms for the entry of an enveloped virus into the cell. Both mechanisms involve fusion of the viral envelope with a cellular membrane, and the end result in both cases is the release of the free nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. 1. Some viruses (ex; measles, HIV) enter by a process called direct fusion. The envelopes of these viruses contain protein spikes that promote fusion of the viral membrane with the plasma membrane of the cell, releasing the nucleocapsid directly into the cytoplasm. 2. Other enveloped viruses (influenza virus, coronavirus), after adsorption, the virus particles are taken up by receptor-mediated endocytosis, which is normally responsible for internalizing growth factors, hormones, and some nutrients. When it involves viruses, the process is referred to as viropexis. The nucleocapsid is now surrounded by two membranes: the original viral envelope and the newly acquired endosomal membrane.

When it involves viruses, the process is referred to as viropexis. The nucleocapsid is now surrounded by two membranes: the original viral envelope and the newly acquired endosomal membrane. Low pH of the endosome leads to a conformational change in a viral spike protein, which results in the fusion of the two membranes and release of the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. All DNA viruses must move from the cytoplasm to the nucleus to replicate, except the poxviruses that replicate in the cytoplasm. A. Transcription & translation An essential step in every virus infection is the production of virus-specific mRNAs that program the cellular ribosomes to synthesize viral proteins. Viral gene expression is often temporally regulated.

Transcription & translation An essential step in every virus infection is the production of virus-specific mRNAs that program the cellular ribosomes to synthesize viral proteins. Viral gene expression is often temporally regulated. Early proteins commonly include regulatory proteins and enzymes needed for genome replication, whereas late proteins are predominantly structural proteins required for assembly of progeny virions. • The genomes of most DNA viruses are transcribed by the host DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RNA polymerase II) in the nucleus to yield the viral mRNAs which are exported to the cytoplasm for translation. • The (+) sense RNA viruses, possess genomes that can be used directly as mRNAs and are translated immediately on entry into the cytoplasm of the cell. • The (–) sense RNA viruses, to make mRNAs must provide their own transcription machinery (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) to produce the viral mRNAs at the beginning of the infection process. Genome replication DNA viruses The extent to which viruses use the cell replication machinery depends on their protein-coding potential and, thus, on the size of their genome. • The smallest of the DNA viruses (parvoviruses) are completely dependent on host machinery that they require the infected cells to be dividing to ensure that a normal S phase occurs and replicates the viral DNA together with the cellular DNA. • The largest DNA viruses (poxviruses) are independent of the host. RNA viruses RNA viruses mostly replicate in the cytoplasm. Moreover, human cells do not have RNA polymerases that can copy RNA templates (RNA-based RNA replication). Therefore, RNA viruses must provide the replicases or polymerases required to duplicate the RNA genome into daughter RNA genomes. 4. Four general principles govern the construction of capsids and nucleocapsids. First, the process generally involves self-assembly of the component parts. Second, assembly is stepwise and ordered. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 7 9 PATHIGENESIS OF VIRAL INFECTION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Distinguish the major routes of viral transmission and entry and relate them to the clinical presentation of viral infections. 2. Explain how viral tropism and host-cell receptor/coreceptor interactions determine the cells and tissues susceptible to viral infection. 3. Analyze the relationships among viral pathogenicity, virulence, cytopathogenicity, and patterns of viral infection in determining clinical disease. 4. Appraise the contribution of host immune responses to virus-induced immunopathology and immunosuppression in selected viral diseases. Viral pathogenesis comprises of several stages, including (1) transmission and entry of the virus into the host, (2) spread in the host, (3) tropism, (4) virulence and cytopathogenicity, (5) patterns of viral infection and disease, (6) virus-induced immunopathology. (7) Virus-induced immunosuppression. 1.

Viral pathogenesis comprises of several stages, including (1) transmission and entry of the virus into the host, (2) spread in the host, (3) tropism, (4) virulence and cytopathogenicity, (5) patterns of viral infection and disease, (6) virus-induced immunopathology. (7) Virus-induced immunosuppression. 1. TRANSMISSION & ENTRY Viruses are transmitted via horizontal (common route of transmission: person to person), and vertical (mother-to-child transmission) routes or vector transmission (from mosquitoes, animals). Human viruses enter the host through a variety of routes, including direct inoculation (break in skin, mucous membranes) as well as respiratory, conjunctival, gastrointestinal, and genital routes. Mother-to-child transmission (vertical transmission) can occur in utero, during delivery (via birth canal), and through breast-feeding. Zoonotic (animal-to-human) transmission of viral infections can occur from the bite of animals (eg, rabies) or insects (eg, dengue, yellow fever) or from inhalation of animal excreta (eg, roboviruses). After virus entry into the host, viruses have variable incubation periods.

Zoonotic (animal-to-human) transmission of viral infections can occur from the bite of animals (eg, rabies) or insects (eg, dengue, yellow fever) or from inhalation of animal excreta (eg, roboviruses). After virus entry into the host, viruses have variable incubation periods. Incubation period is the time between exposure to the organism and appearance of the first symptoms of the disease. Viruses generally multiply at the site of entry to establish infection in the host. Some viruses have short incubation periods (influenza—2-4 days), whereas others have long incubation periods (eg, hepatitis B virus—weeks to several months). 2. SPREAD IN THE HOST • Viral infections produce either localized infection at the site of entry or disseminated infection spread throughout the body. • Localized infections include influenza, parainfluenza, common cold (rhinoviruses, coronaviruses), gastrointestinal infections (rotaviruses), and skin infections (papillomaviruses). In localized infections, the virus spreads mainly by infecting adjacent or neighboring cells.

• Localized infections include influenza, parainfluenza, common cold (rhinoviruses, coronaviruses), gastrointestinal infections (rotaviruses), and skin infections (papillomaviruses). In localized infections, the virus spreads mainly by infecting adjacent or neighboring cells. • Several viruses that cause systemic disease in the host spread from the site of entry to the target tissue, where they cause cell injury after multiplication. Viruses use two major routes to spread and cause systemic infection, that is, hematogenous (via the bloodstream) and NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 7 neural (via neurons) spread. Some of the viruses that cause systemic or disseminated infection are poliovirus, rabies virus, HBV, HCV, HIV, measles, varicella zoster virus, and others. 3. TROPISM • Tropism is the capability of viruses to infect a discrete population of cells within an organ. • Cellular or tissue tropism is most often determined by the specific interaction of viral surface proteins (spikes) and cellular receptors on the host cells.

TROPISM • Tropism is the capability of viruses to infect a discrete population of cells within an organ. • Cellular or tissue tropism is most often determined by the specific interaction of viral surface proteins (spikes) and cellular receptors on the host cells. However, it should be kept in mind that the presence of a receptor for a virus is not always sufficient for viral infection in the target cells. For example, the presence of CD4 (HIV receptor) alone on target cells does not allow virus entry into these cells, but it requires that target cells also express coreceptors, CXCR4 or CCR5 (chemokine receptors) for efficient viral attachment. • Different viruses may use the same cellular molecule as receptors. Some examples are sialic acid residues functioning as important components of the receptor for influenza, corona. 4. VIRULENCE AND CYTOPATHOGENICITY • Pathogenicity: The ability of a virus to cause disease in an infected host. • Viral virulence: is the degree of pathogenicity of a virus. A virus may be of high or low virulence for a particular host. Different strains of the same virus may differ in the degree of pathogenicity.

• Viral virulence: is the degree of pathogenicity of a virus. A virus may be of high or low virulence for a particular host. Different strains of the same virus may differ in the degree of pathogenicity. • Cytopathogenicity: The ability of a virus to cause degenerative changes in cells or cell death. • Virulent viruses: Viral strains that kill target cells and cause disease. • Avirulent or attenuated strains: strains that have mutated and lost their ability to cause cytopathic effects (CPE) and disease. Some attenuated strains can be used as live vaccines. • Interference: If two closely related viruses infect a host, then infection by the first virus can inhibit the function of the second virus Replication of the virus results in alterations of cellular morphology and function as well as antigenicity of the virus. When a lytic virus infects a permissive cell, lots of daughter viruses are produced and this is followed by lysis of the infected cells, called cytopathic effects (CPE) of the virus. The features of CPE are morphologic changes of the cell (inclusion bodies, thickening of the nucleus, swelling, cell fusion [syncytia]), followed by cellular lysis.

When a lytic virus infects a permissive cell, lots of daughter viruses are produced and this is followed by lysis of the infected cells, called cytopathic effects (CPE) of the virus. The features of CPE are morphologic changes of the cell (inclusion bodies, thickening of the nucleus, swelling, cell fusion [syncytia]), followed by cellular lysis. Some viruses encode a new class of proteins called virokines and viroreceptors, which contribute to viral virulence by mimicking cellular proteins. Virokines are secreted from infected cells and act as cytokines, helping the cells to proliferate and increase virus production. Viroreceptors resemble cytokine receptors and attract cellular cytokines. E.g. Herpesviruses 5. PATTERNS OF VIRAL INFECTION & DISEASE Three major outcomes can be attributed to a viral infection: (1) abortive infection, in which no progeny virus particles are produced, but the cell may die because early viral functions can occur. (2) lytic infection, in which active virus production is followed by cell death. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A.

PATTERNS OF VIRAL INFECTION & DISEASE Three major outcomes can be attributed to a viral infection: (1) abortive infection, in which no progeny virus particles are produced, but the cell may die because early viral functions can occur. (2) lytic infection, in which active virus production is followed by cell death. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 7 (3) persistent infection, in which small numbers of virus particles are produced with little or no CPE. Persistent infections include: a. latent infection, in which viral genetic material remains in host cell without production of virus and may be activated at a later time to produce virus and/or transform the host cell. b. chronic infection, which involves low level of virus production with little or no CPE; and viral transformation, in which viral infection or viral gene product induces unregulated cellular growth, and cells form tumors in the host. Based on patterns and levels of detectable infectious virus in the host and the role of immune response in clearing the virus, viral infections can be divided into five categories: (Figure 1) (1) acute infection that is cleared by the immune response.

Based on patterns and levels of detectable infectious virus in the host and the role of immune response in clearing the virus, viral infections can be divided into five categories: (Figure 1) (1) acute infection that is cleared by the immune response. In acute infection, the virus enters the host, then multiplies at the site of entry and in the target tissue, and this is followed by viremia and cytopathic effects. This type of infection is a lytic infection. The immune system mounts both cellular and humoral responses and successfully eliminates the virus from the host. Examples of acute viral infections followed by clearance of the virus from the host by immune responses are hepatitis A, influenza, parainfluenza, rhino, and corona viruses. (2) acute infection that becomes latent and periodically reactivated. In some viral infections, acute infection may result in either asymptomatic or symptomatic disease followed by latent infection in which the viral genome persists without any infectious virus production.

text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 10 ANTIVIRAL AGENTS & RESISTANCE ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Classify antiviral agents according to their molecular target and stage of the viral replication cycle. 2. Explain the relationship between the mechanism of action of selected antiviral agents and their clinical indications. 3. Select an appropriate antiviral agent for a patient according to the causative virus, mechanism of action, and clinically relevant drug characteristics. 4. Analyze the causes and clinical consequences of antiviral resistance and appropriate strategies to minimize or manage it. Unlike viruses, bacteria do not rely on host cellular machinery for replication, so processes specific to these organisms provide ideal targets for the development of antibacterial drugs. Because viruses are obligate intracellular parasites, antiviral agents must be capable of selectively inhibiting viral functions without damaging the host, making the development of such drugs very difficult.

Because viruses are obligate intracellular parasites, antiviral agents must be capable of selectively inhibiting viral functions without damaging the host, making the development of such drugs very difficult. Another limitation is that many rounds of virus replication occur during the incubation period and the virus has spread before symptoms appear, making drug treatment after the development of clinical symptoms relatively ineffective. Thus, the challenges in the development of antiviral agents is identification of the steps in viral replication that are unique to the virus and not used by the normal cell. Among the unique viral events are attachment, penetration, uncoating, RNA-directed DNA synthesis (reverse transcription) or RNA-directed RNA synthesis (RNA viruses), and assembly and release of the intact virion. There is a need for antiviral drugs active against viruses for which vaccines are not available or not highly effective because of a multiplicity of serotypes (eg, rhinoviruses) or because of constantly changing viral antigens (eg, influenza, HIV).

There is a need for antiviral drugs active against viruses for which vaccines are not available or not highly effective because of a multiplicity of serotypes (eg, rhinoviruses) or because of constantly changing viral antigens (eg, influenza, HIV). Antivirals are usually most effective when started early, because viral replication may peak before or around symptom onset. Clinical benefit depends on the virus, site of infection, host factors, and timing. Combination therapy is particularly important for viruses with high mutation rates, such as HIV and HCV, because it suppresses replication more effectively and reduces the probability of resistance. Meheissen Page 2 of 5 SELECTED ANTIVIRAL AGENTS 1. Inhibitors of Uncoating Amantadine and rimantadine, which are thought to inhibit viral uncoating as their primary antiviral effect. They are extremely selective, with activity against only influenza A, where they act as inhibitors of the viral M2 protein. They have been used either as prophylaxis or for therapy. Unfortunately, since 2001, the rates of resistance to amantadine/rimantadine have increased so sharply (up to 100% for some strains) that they are no longer routinely recommended. 2. Fusion inhibitors HIV fusion inhibitors act by disrupting the fusion of viral envelope with the cell membrane, preventing cellular infection. The prototype agent is enfuvirtide. 3. Inhibitors of nucleic acid synthesis a. Nucleoside analogues Most antiviral agents are nucleoside analogues that are active against virus-specific nucleic acid polymerases or reverse transcriptases and have much less activity against analogueous host enzymes. Some of these agents serve as nucleic acid chain terminators after incorporation into nucleic acids.

Nucleoside analogues Most antiviral agents are nucleoside analogues that are active against virus-specific nucleic acid polymerases or reverse transcriptases and have much less activity against analogueous host enzymes. Some of these agents serve as nucleic acid chain terminators after incorporation into nucleic acids. Nucleoside analogues cause selective inhibition of viral replication: § by binding better to viral DNA polymerase, rather than to the cellular DNA polymerase; and § by being utilized more extensively in virus-infected cells due to the more rapid synthesis of DNA in infected cells. 1. Acyclovir A guanosine analogue. The key to its benefit is that it must be phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase to be active. Therefore, the compound is essentially nontoxic because it is not phosphorylated or activated in uninfected host cells. Viral thymidine kinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of acyclovir to a monophosphate, then host cell enzymes complete the progression to the diphosphate and, finally, the triphosphate. Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral replication by competing with guanosine triphosphate and inhibiting the function of the virally encoded DNA polymerase.

Viral thymidine kinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of acyclovir to a monophosphate, then host cell enzymes complete the progression to the diphosphate and, finally, the triphosphate. Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral replication by competing with guanosine triphosphate and inhibiting the function of the virally encoded DNA polymerase. Susceptible strains of herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1 and -2) are the most active thymidine kinase inducers and are the most readily inhibited by acyclovir. Resistant strains of HSV have been recovered from immunocompromised patients, including patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS); in most instances, resistance results from mutations in the viral thymidine kinase gene or viral DNA polymerase. 2. Ganciclovir A guanosine analogue. It confers activity against cytomegalovirus (CMV). Acyclovir has low activity against CMV because it is not well phosphorylated in CMV-infected cells due to the absence of the gene for thymidine kinase in CMV.

It confers activity against cytomegalovirus (CMV). Acyclovir has low activity against CMV because it is not well phosphorylated in CMV-infected cells due to the absence of the gene for thymidine kinase in CMV. However, ganciclovir is active against CMV because another viral-encoded phosphorylating enzyme (UL97) is present in CMV-infected cells that is, capable of phosphorylating ganciclovir and converting it to the monophosphate. Then, cellular enzymes convert it to the active compound, ganciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits the viral DNA polymerase. Since NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. The basis for the relatively selective therapeutic effect of AZT is that HIV reverse transcriptase is more than 100 times more sensitive to AZT than is host cell DNA polymerase. It is also used for treatment of pregnant HIV-infected women. It has been shown to reduce or prevent the transmission of HIV from the mother to the baby. The drug, however, is toxic and costly. 4. Lamivudine Lamivudine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor with activity against HIV and HBV to disrupt viral DNA synthesis. Lamivudine is phosphorylated intracellularly to its active triphosphate metabolite. This nucleoside analogueue is incorporated into viral DNA by HIV reverse transcriptase and HBV polymerase, resulting in DNA chain termination. 5. Ribavirin A guanosine analogue. Similar to other nucleoside analogues, ribavirin must be phosphorylated to mono, di-, and triphosphate forms, but cellular enzymes can carry out each of these, thus, heightening the risk of toxicity. It is an inhibitor of RNA polymerase. It was used used in treatment of HCV.

Similar to other nucleoside analogues, ribavirin must be phosphorylated to mono, di-, and triphosphate forms, but cellular enzymes can carry out each of these, thus, heightening the risk of toxicity. It is an inhibitor of RNA polymerase. It was used used in treatment of HCV. Aerosol administration is used for treatment of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). 6. Idoxuridine and Trifluorothymidine Idoxuridine blocks nucleic acid synthesis by being incorporated into DNA in place of thymidine and producing a non- functional molecule. It is phosphorylated by cellular thymidine kinase to the active compound, which inhibits both viral and cellular DNA polymerase. The resulting host toxicity precludes systemic administration in humans. Idoxuridine can be used topically as effective treatment of herpetic keratitis. Trifluorothymidine, a related pyrimidine analogue, is effective in treating herpetic corneal infections, including those that fail to respond to Idoxuridine. Figure 1. text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 7 11 INTRODUCTION TO MEDICAL MYCOLOGY ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Interpret the major morphological features of medically important fungi and relate them to their mode of growth and pathogenic potential. 2. Differentiate superficial, subcutaneous, systemic, and opportunistic mycoses using clinical presentation, host factors, and tissue involvement. 3. Apply appropriate laboratory diagnostic approaches to common superficial and opportunistic fungal infections based on specimen type and fungal characteristics. 4. Analyze the relationship between fungal virulence mechanisms, host immune status, route of transmission, and the resulting clinical manifestations. Medical mycology is the study of fungi that cause human disease, including their morphology, classification, pathogenesis, laboratory diagnosis, treatment and prevention. Differences of Fungi from bacteria • Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with a true nucleus. • They have chitin and β-glucans in the cell wall. • The cell membrane contains ergosterol, an important antifungal drug target.

Differences of Fungi from bacteria • Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with a true nucleus. • They have chitin and β-glucans in the cell wall. • The cell membrane contains ergosterol, an important antifungal drug target. • Most pathogenic fungi grow more slowly than bacteria. • Fungi reproduce by asexual (production of spores, budding) and/or sexual spores (production of zygotes).. • Fungal spores are important for environmental survival and transmission, but they should not be confused with bacterial endospores. Structure of fungal cell The fungal cell has many typical eukaryotic features, including a nucleus with a nucleolus, nuclear membrane, and linear chromosomes. The cytoplasm contains a cytoskeleton, ribosomes and organelles, such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and the Golgi apparatus. Fungal cells have a rigid cell wall (made of complex polysaccharides such as mannans, glucans, and chitins in close association with each other and with structural proteins) external to the cytoplasmic membrane (made of ergosterol). Mannoproteins of the cell wall are composed of mannan found on the cell surface where they are linked to various proteins.

Fungal cells have a rigid cell wall (made of complex polysaccharides such as mannans, glucans, and chitins in close association with each other and with structural proteins) external to the cytoplasmic membrane (made of ergosterol). Mannoproteins of the cell wall are composed of mannan found on the cell surface where they are linked to various proteins. Mannoproteins are very important since antibodies are readily developed against these molecules on the cell surface. Figure 1. Structure of fungal cell NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 7 Morphology & classification of fungi The size of fungi varies from bacterial size (2-4 μm) to a macroscopically visible structure. The morphologic forms of growth vary from colonies superficially resembling those of bacteria to some of the most complex, multicellular, colorful, structures seen in nature. Fungi that cause human infections can be divided based on their morphological forms into: 1. Yeasts are fungi that primarily grow in a round cellular form. The yeasts tend to have the simplest cellular forms, reproducing by a process of asexual budding, constriction, and cell separation similar to many bacteria. e.g.

Yeasts are fungi that primarily grow in a round cellular form. The yeasts tend to have the simplest cellular forms, reproducing by a process of asexual budding, constriction, and cell separation similar to many bacteria. e.g. Cryptococcus 2. Molds are fungi that primarily grow as filamentous, tube-like structures called hyphae. As the hyphae extend, they form an intertwined mass called a mycelium. Most molds form hyphal septa, which are cross-walls perpendicular to the cell walls, dividing the hypha into subunit cells (septate molds), others do not form septa (aseptate molds). They reproduce asexually (spores), or sexually (zygote). e.g. Aspergillus 3. Pseudohyphae which are actually elongated yeast cells growing end-to-end. Pseudohyphae are distinguished from true hyphae by having recurring bud-like constrictions and less rigid cell walls. e.g. Candida. 4. Dimorphic can transition between morphological forms depending on environmental conditions.

Pseudohyphae are distinguished from true hyphae by having recurring bud-like constrictions and less rigid cell walls. e.g. Candida. 4. Dimorphic can transition between morphological forms depending on environmental conditions. A distinct group of human pathogens are the thermally dimorphic fungi, shifting from tissue-associated form (as yeast-like) (37°C) in mammalian host to hyphal growth (ambient temperature) in their environmental reservoir, based on temperature. e.g. Histoplasma capsulatum Yeasts Figure 2. Morphology of fungi Grouping of medically important fungi based on the types of tissues they infect and the diseases they produce, is as follows: 1. The superficial mycoses, such as the dermatophytes, cause indolent lesions of the skin and its appendages, commonly known as ringworm and athlete’s foot, without typically spreading to deeper tissues. 2. The subcutaneous mycoses characteristically cause infection through the skin, followed by subcutaneous or lymphatic spread. e.g. mycetoma NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 7 3.

The subcutaneous mycoses characteristically cause infection through the skin, followed by subcutaneous or lymphatic spread. e.g. mycetoma NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 7 3. The opportunistic mycoses are those found in the environment or in the resident flora that produce disease primarily in immunocompromised hosts. E.g. Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis, Mucor. 4. The systemic mycoses are the most virulent fungi and may cause serious and progressive systemic disease in previously healthy persons. They are not found in the human microbiota. Although their major potential is to produce deep-seated visceral infections and systemic spread. e.g. Histoplasma N.B. Many opportunistic fungal infections are primarily diseases of patients with impaired host defenses rather than highly virulent pathogens in healthy individuals. Figure 3. Dermatophytes causing superficial mycoses Figure 4. Fungi causing opportunistic mycoses NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 7 Infections caused by fungi The diseases caused by fungi are called mycoses.

Meheissen Page 4 of 7 Infections caused by fungi The diseases caused by fungi are called mycoses. These infections vary greatly in their manifestations but tend to present with subacute or chronic features, often relapsing over time. Acute disease, such as that produced by many viruses and bacteria, is uncommon with fungal infections. 1. Superficial mycoses Dermatophytes General term for species invading superficial layers of skin. Of the many species involved, those belonging to Epidermophyton, Microsporum and Trichophyton are of greatest importance. Characteristics Filamentous fungi invading surface keratinized structures: skin, hair, nails. Hyphae penetrate between cells. Dermatophytes utilize keratin and generally remain in keratinized tissues rather than invading viable tissue. Epidermophyton → skin and nails, not hair Microsporum → skin and hair, generally not nails Trichophyton → skin, hair and nails Transmission By contact with fungal material on skin scales.

Epidermophyton → skin and nails, not hair Microsporum → skin and hair, generally not nails Trichophyton → skin, hair and nails Transmission By contact with fungal material on skin scales. Pathogenesis Skin inflammation, pruritus – sometimes localized hypersensitivity reactions. Diseases Tinea, ringworm, athlete’s foot. Laboratory identification Examination of KOH-treated skin scrapings for hyphae; fluorescence under Wood’s lamp. Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) Treatment Topical (imidazoles) and oral antifungal agents (griseofulvin, itraconazole, terbinafine). 2. Opportunistic mycoses A. Aspergillus spp. Aspergillus species are molds found readily in the environment. Invasive aspergillosis occurs in highly immunocompromised persons, often rapidly resulting in death. Aspergillus fumigatus is the most important of three common species, the others being Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus niger. Characteristics Filamentous fungi causing opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients. Occur widely in external environment. Invade lungs and blood vessels. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 5 of 7 Transmission Inhalation of airborne conidia.

Occur widely in external environment. Invade lungs and blood vessels. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 5 of 7 Transmission Inhalation of airborne conidia. Pathogenesis Causes thrombosis and infarction when blood vessels invaded. Partial blockage of airways from fungal mass. Allergic bronchopulmonary reactions. Host factors favoring Aspergillus growth include anatomic abnormalities of the lungs (eg, bronchiectasis, severe emphysema) and immunosuppression (neutropenia, lung transplantation). Diseases Aspergillus fumigatus: pulmonary aspergillosis; 1) Aspergillus pneumonia, (2) disseminated aspergillosis, (3) allergic respiratory disease, and (4)aspergilloma (fungus ball).
