NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 4 12 ANTIFUNGAL AGENTS & RESISTANCE ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Differentiate the mechanisms of action of major antifungal drug classes based on their fungal cellular targets. 2. Interpret the clinical spectrum and pharmacologic properties of antifungal agents to guide treatment of common and life-threatening fungal infections. 3. Select an appropriate antifungal agent for a patient according to the fungal pathogen, site/severity of infection, and important drug toxicities. 4. Analyze antifungal resistance mechanisms by relating changes in drug targets, drug uptake, efflux, or biosynthetic pathways to therapeutic failure. Compared with antibacterial agents, relatively few antifungals are available for treatment of fungal infections. Many substances with antifungal activity have proved to be unstable, to be toxic to humans, or to have undesirable pharmacologic characteristics, such as poor diffusion into tissues. Newer antifungal agents target fungal-specific cellular features and demonstrate lower toxicity than older drug classes. 1. Antifungals acting on cytoplasmic membrane A.

Many substances with antifungal activity have proved to be unstable, to be toxic to humans, or to have undesirable pharmacologic characteristics, such as poor diffusion into tissues. Newer antifungal agents target fungal-specific cellular features and demonstrate lower toxicity than older drug classes. 1. Antifungals acting on cytoplasmic membrane A. Polyenes Action: The polyenes nystatin and amphotericin B are lipophilic and bind to ergosterol, the dominant sterol in the cytoplasmic membrane of fungal cells. After binding, they form annular channels, which penetrate the membrane and lead to leakage of essential small molecules from the cytoplasm and cell death. Spectrum of activity: Almost all fungi are susceptible to amphotericin B, and the development of resistance is rare. Use of amphotericin B is limited to progressive, life-threatening fungal infections. Amphotericin B is insoluble in water and must be administered intravenously as a colloidal suspension. Side effects: The major limitation to amphotericin B therapy is the toxicity created by its affinity for mammalian as well as fungal membranes.

Amphotericin B is insoluble in water and must be administered intravenously as a colloidal suspension. Side effects: The major limitation to amphotericin B therapy is the toxicity created by its affinity for mammalian as well as fungal membranes. Intravenous Infusion is commonly followed by chills, fever, headache, and dyspnea. The most serious toxic effect is renal dysfunction. The even greater toxicity of nystatin limits its use to topical preparations. Preparations that complex amphotericin B with lipids (liposomal amphotericin) have been used as a means to limit toxicity. B. Azoles Action: Their activity is based on inhibition of the enzyme “lanosterol 14-α-demethylase” responsible for conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, the major component of the fungal cell membrane. This leads to ergosterol depletion and lanosterol accumulation, forming defective membranes. Azoles are generally fungistatic against many fungi rather than uniformly fungicidal. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 4 Spectrum of activity: Fluconazole is primarily active against yeasts, including many Cryptococcus and Candida species.

NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 4 Spectrum of activity: Fluconazole is primarily active against yeasts, including many Cryptococcus and Candida species. Mold-active azoles (itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole) have extended activity against molds such as Aspergillus species. These Most of these agents can be given orally or parenterally. Topical agents (ketoconazole, clotrimazole, and miconazole) are available as topical preparations for superficial mycoses. Side effects: Azoles can cause varying degrees of liver toxicity. Additionally, many systemic azoles, can adversely affect cardiac myocyte repolarization and therefore prolong the QTc interval on an ECG, placing patients at increased risk for cardiac arrhythmias. Azoles can also affect the precursors of some hormones and may therefore cause endocrinological side effects, restricting their use in pregnancy. C. Allylamaines Action: The allylamines act by inhibition of an enzyme (squalene epoxidase) in the early stages of ergosterol synthesis. Spectrum of activity: The allylamine group includes an oral and topical agent.

Allylamaines Action: The allylamines act by inhibition of an enzyme (squalene epoxidase) in the early stages of ergosterol synthesis. Spectrum of activity: The allylamine group includes an oral and topical agent. Terbinafine is particularly effective against dermatophytes and accumulates in keratinized tissues, making it an important treatment for tinea infections and onychomycosis. 2. Antifungals acting on nucleic acid synthesis Action: 5-Flucytosine (5FC) is an analog of cytosine. It is a potent inhibitor of RNA transcription and DNA synthesis. Spectrum of activity: Flucytosine is well absorbed after oral administration. It is active against most clinically important yeasts, including Candida albicans and Cryptococcus neoformans, but it has little activity against molds. Side effects: The frequent development of mutational resistance during therapy limits its application to mild yeast infections or its use in combination with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis. The primary toxic effect of flucytosine is a reversible bone marrow suppression that can lead to neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. 3.

Side effects: The frequent development of mutational resistance during therapy limits its application to mild yeast infections or its use in combination with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis. The primary toxic effect of flucytosine is a reversible bone marrow suppression that can lead to neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. 3. Antifungals acting on cell wall synthesis The unique chemical nature of the fungal cell wall, with its interwoven layers of mannans, glucans, and chitin, makes it an ideal target for chemotherapeutic attack. The echinocandins, which block glucan synthesis, are now in widespread clinical use due to their potent antifungal effect and comparatively low adverse effect profile. Other cell wall-active antifungals are in preclinical development. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 4 Echinocandins Action: Echinocandins inhibit a glucan biosynthetic enzyme (β-1,3-D-glucan synthase) required for the synthesis of fungal cell wall. Echinocandin administration, therefore, causes morphologic distortions and osmotic instability in yeasts and molds, similar to the effect of β-lactams on bacteria.

Meheissen Page 3 of 4 Echinocandins Action: Echinocandins inhibit a glucan biosynthetic enzyme (β-1,3-D-glucan synthase) required for the synthesis of fungal cell wall. Echinocandin administration, therefore, causes morphologic distortions and osmotic instability in yeasts and molds, similar to the effect of β-lactams on bacteria. Spectrum of activity: Caspofungin, has activity against Candida and Aspergillus. Although highly active against many Candida species, the echinocandins tend to be used as second-line agents for invasive aspergillosis. Cryptococcus neoformans whose cell wall glucans have a slightly different structure, are more tolerant of echinocandins. Newer echinocandins, micafungin and anidulafungin, have the same mode of action and a similar spectrum of antifungal activity. Side effects: Since there are no similar glucans in humans, echinocandin toxicity is minimal. 4. Others Griseofulvin Action: acts on the microtubules and associated proteins that make up the mitotic spindle. It interferes with cell division. Spectrum of activity: after oral administration, it is absorbed from GIT and concentrates in the keratinized layers of the skin.

Others Griseofulvin Action: acts on the microtubules and associated proteins that make up the mitotic spindle. It interferes with cell division. Spectrum of activity: after oral administration, it is absorbed from GIT and concentrates in the keratinized layers of the skin. It is active only against the agents of superficial mycoses. Side effects: Clinical response is slow. Prolonged therapy may be required. Antifungal resistance Many of the same resistance mechanisms observed in bacteria are also found in fungi. Fungi tend to primarily inactivate drug activity using efflux pumps and by altering their biosynthetic pathways. In contrast to bacteria, fungi do not make hydrolytic enzymes to inactivate antibiotics to the same extent as bacteria. Polyene Resistance Because amphotericin B binds directly to the ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, the only means to resist this action is to change the membrane sterol composition. Therefore, resistance is rare. Flucytosine Resistance Flucytosine (5-FC) requires a permease for entry into the cell and then multiple enzymes to modify it to the active metabolites that inhibit nucleic acid synthesis.

Flucytosine Resistance Flucytosine (5-FC) requires a permease for entry into the cell and then multiple enzymes to modify it to the active metabolites that inhibit nucleic acid synthesis. Mutation in any one of these enzymes renders the drug ineffective. This is the reason that its use is mostly limited to combination therapy with other antifungals. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 4 of 4 Azole Resistance The most well-characterized mechanism is through the induction of efflux pumps that transport the drug out of the cell. Mutation of demethylase enzyme, effectively decreasing the affinity of the azole for its enzyme target. Some azole-resistant strains have also been shown to accomplish ergosterol synthesis by an alternate pathway, thus bypassing the azole target enzyme. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 6 13 PRINCIPLES OF VACCINES ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Explain the immunological principles underlying vaccination and vaccine-induced protection in clinical contexts. 2. Differentiate major vaccine platforms according to their composition, immune response, advantages, limitations, and clinical applications. 3. Interpret clinical situations to select an appropriate vaccine type based on host factors, route of administration, and expected immune response. 4. Evaluate the benefits and limitations of vaccination strategies, including herd immunity, adjuvant use, conjugation, and vaccine interference. What is a vaccine? The word “vaccine” originates from the Latin Variolae vaccinae (cowpox), which Edward Jenner demonstrated in 1798 could prevent smallpox in humans. Today the term ‘vaccine’ applies to all biological preparations, produced from living organisms, that enhance immunity against disease and either prevent (prophylactic vaccines) or, in some cases, treat disease (therapeutic vaccines).

Today the term ‘vaccine’ applies to all biological preparations, produced from living organisms, that enhance immunity against disease and either prevent (prophylactic vaccines) or, in some cases, treat disease (therapeutic vaccines). Vaccines are administered in liquid form, either by injection, by oral, or by intranasal routes. Principle of vaccination -Vaccines artificially stimulate immunity through exposure to an antigenic substance. An effective vaccine does not protect against disease until it is administered in the proper dosage to susceptible individuals. -Vaccination is a form of active immunization in which exposure to a vaccine antigen stimulates the recipient's own adaptive immune response, producing immunological memory and protection against subsequent infection or disease. - The major goal of vaccination is to generate immunological memory through activation of antigen-specific B and T lymphocytes. Subsequent exposure to the pathogen produces a faster and stronger secondary immune response, which prevents infection, severe disease, or complications.

- The major goal of vaccination is to generate immunological memory through activation of antigen-specific B and T lymphocytes. Subsequent exposure to the pathogen produces a faster and stronger secondary immune response, which prevents infection, severe disease, or complications. -Vaccines may protect by inducing neutralizing antibodies, opsonizing antibodies, cytotoxic T-cell responses, mucosal immunity, or combinations of these mechanisms, depending on the pathogen and vaccine platform. Herd immunity refers to the fact that the risk of infection among susceptible individuals in a population is reduced by the presence of adequate numbers of immune individuals. However, the threshold of immunity needed for this indirect protective effect depends on many factors, including the transmissibility of the infectious agent, the nature of the vaccine-induced immunity, and the distribution of the immune individuals. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 6 Figure 1. What is herd immunity? Vaccines are composed of either the entire disease-causing microorganism or some of its components.

NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 6 Figure 1. What is herd immunity? Vaccines are composed of either the entire disease-causing microorganism or some of its components. They may be constructed in several ways: • From living organisms that have been weakened, usually from cultivation under sub-optimal conditions (also called attenuation), or from genetic modification, which has the effect of reducing their ability to cause disease; • From whole organisms that have been inactivated by chemical, thermal or other means; • From components of the disease-causing organism, such as specific proteins and polysaccharides, or nucleic acid • From inactivated toxins of toxin-producing bacteria, called toxoid. • From the conjugation of polysaccharides to proteins (this increases the effectiveness of polysaccharide vaccines in young children) Types of Vaccines 1. Whole-organism vaccines – live attenuated or inactivated 2. Component/subunit vaccines – protein, polysaccharide, toxoid and conjugate vaccines. 3. Recombinant and vector-based vaccines 4. Nucleic-acid vaccines – DNA and mRNA vaccines A.

Whole-organism vaccines – live attenuated or inactivated 2. Component/subunit vaccines – protein, polysaccharide, toxoid and conjugate vaccines. 3. Recombinant and vector-based vaccines 4. Nucleic-acid vaccines – DNA and mRNA vaccines A. Live Attenuated Vaccines Live vaccines use mutants that antigenically overlap with wild-type organism but are restricted in some step in the pathogenesis of disease. These wild viruses or bacteria are attenuated (weakened) in a laboratory, by serial passages in animals or cell cultures. As more is learned about microbial genes involved in disease pathogenesis, attenuated vaccines can be engineered in the laboratory. To produce an immune response, live, attenuated vaccines must replicate in the vaccinated person. Attenuated live vaccines have the advantage of acting more like the natural infection with regard to their effect on immunity. Because live attenuated organisms replicate within the host, they can activate both MHC class I and class II pathways, resulting in both cellular and humoral immune responses. When administered through a mucosal route, live attenuated vaccines can stimulate local secretory IgA and mucosal immune responses.

Because live attenuated organisms replicate within the host, they can activate both MHC class I and class II pathways, resulting in both cellular and humoral immune responses. When administered through a mucosal route, live attenuated vaccines can stimulate local secretory IgA and mucosal immune responses. Disadvantages of attenuated live vaccines include (1) a risk of reversion to greater virulence, (2) severe infection in immunocompromised hosts, and (3) limited storage and shelf life in some cases (destroyed by heat and light). (4) Active immunity from a live, attenuated vaccine may not develop because of interference with the vaccine virus by NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 6 circulating antibody. Antibody from any source (e.g., transplacental transfer to infants, transfusion of blood products) can interfere with replication of the vaccine organism and lead to poor response or no response to the vaccine. The live, attenuated viral vaccines as MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), varicella. Bacterial live attenuated vaccines as typhoid vaccine (Ty21a), and Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG). B.

The live, attenuated viral vaccines as MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), varicella. Bacterial live attenuated vaccines as typhoid vaccine (Ty21a), and Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG). B. Inactivated (killed) vaccines They are made by purifying bacterial or viral preparations to a certain extent and then inactivating their infectivity in a way that does minimal damage to the important proteins; mild chemical (formalin) or thermal treatment is frequently used. Adjuvant is added to boost the immunogenicity, as they enhance uptake by presenting cells e.g. aluminium hydroxide or aluminium phosphate. [Adjuvants enhance vaccine immunogenicity by promoting innate immune activation, antigen uptake and presentation, and cytokine production. They may allow a stronger and more durable adaptive immune response and can reduce the amount of antigen required per vaccine dose]. The immunity provided by inactivated vaccines is generally not as long-lasting as that obtained from live, attenuated vaccines. Multiple doses over time are needed to obtain ongoing immunity.

Unlike live vaccines, which produce an immune response that closely resembles natural infection, the immune response to an inactivated vaccine is mostly antibody production. Little or no cellular immunity results. As a result, some inactivated vaccines may require periodic supplemental doses (Booster doses). Advantages of inactivated vaccines are that there is no reversion to virulence by the vaccine form. Disadvantages of inactivated vaccines include relatively brief immunity requiring boosting shots to maintain effectiveness, poor cell-mediated response. Staphylococcus aureus Characteristics Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Some strains produce capsules. Non-fastidious; facultative anaerobe (capable of aerobic and anaerobic respiration) Transmission Normal habitat: humans (and animals associated with them); skin, especially nose and perineum (carriage rates higher in hospital patients and staff). Spread is mainly by contact. Pathogenesis Virulence multifactorial: • cell-associated: capsule, protein A, fibronectin-binding protein, collagen-binding proteins • many strains have protein A bound to the mucopeptide of the cell wall. This protein interacts non-specifically with host IgG antibodies reducing opsonization and causing local activation of complement. • Enzymes: coagulase, catalase.

text: NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 4 15 GRAM NEGATIVE BACILLI OF MEDICAL IMPORTANCE ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Differentiate clinically important Gram-negative bacilli according to their characteristic microbiological, epidemiological, and clinical features. 2. Introduction • Gram-negative bacteria are among the world's most significant public health problems due to their high resistance to antibiotics. These microorganisms have significant clinical importance in hospitals because they often require patients to be in the intensive care unit (ICU), and patients are at high risk of morbidity and mortality.

text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Characteristics Aerobic Gram-negative rod, motile by means of polar flagella. Able to utilize a very wide range of carbon and energy sources and to grow over a wide temperature range. Does not ferment carbohydrates. Transmission P. aeruginosa is widespread in moist areas in the environment; patients usually become infected by contact spread, directly or indirectly, from these environmental sites. Pathogenesis A number of virulence factors have been identified, including endotoxin and exotoxin A, which acts as an inhibitor of elongation factor in eukaryotic protein synthesis. Extracellular polysaccharide capsule helps to prevent phagocytosis (e.g. massive amounts of alginate produced by strains specifically in cystic fibrosis patients). Pigments may have a role in pathogenicity. Diseases P. aeruginosa is an opportunist pathogen that can infect almost any body site given the right predisposing conditions. It causes infections of skin and burns, it is a major lung pathogen in cystic fibrosis, and can cause pneumonia in intubated patients. It can also cause UTIs, septicaemia, osteomyelitis and endocarditis.

Patients usually become infected by contact spread, directly or indirectly, from these environmental sites. Diseases Opportunistic pathogen causing infections in the respiratory tract, urinary tract, wounds, and sepsis Laboratory identification Gram stain morphology is characteristic—large, Gram variable coccobacilli. Treatment Treatment must be guided by in vitro susceptibility tests because multidrug resistance is common.

text: Page 1 of 6 L16 Introduction to Medical Parasitology SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Identify the concept of Parasitology. 2. Define the terms related to human – parasite relationship. 3. Differentiate between types of parasites and hosts. 4. Discuss the pathogenesis of parasitic diseases. 5. Classify parasites of medical importance. What is Parasitology It is the study of parasites and their relationship to their hosts. It is one of the most fascinating areas of biology. It is entirely proper to classify many bacteria and fungi and all viruses as parasites, however, Parasitology has traditionally been limited to parasitic protozoa, helminths, and arthropods. Global Importance of Parasitology The World Health Organization (WHO) has declared that five out of six major unbeaten human tropical diseases are parasitic. They are schistosomiasis, malaria, filariasis, African trypanosomiasis, and leishmaniasis. NB: Leprosy is the sixth major disease caused by a bacterium. Host -Parasite relationship Symbiosis Literally, the word symbiosis means “living together”.

text: They are schistosomiasis, malaria, filariasis, African trypanosomiasis, and leishmaniasis. NB: Leprosy is the sixth major disease caused by a bacterium. Host -Parasite relationship Symbiosis Literally, the word symbiosis means “living together”. When the two organisms (partners) live in close association, commonly one living in or on the body of the other, they are termed to be symbiotic, as contrasted with free-living organisms. Each of these two organisms is termed a symbiont. Usually, but not necessarily, the symbionts are of different species. Mutualism Mutualism describes a type of symbiosis in which both partners benefit from the association. Mutualism is usually obligatory since in most cases physiological dependence has evolved to such a degree that one organism cannot survive without the other. Page 2 of 6 Commensalism Another type of symbiosis in which one partner benefits from the association, but the other is neither helped nor harmed. The term means “eating at the same table,” and many commens Mutualism describes a type of symbiosis in which both partners benefit from the association. al relationships involve feeding on the wasted food of the host.

Parasitism It is a symbiotic relationship in which one of the partners, the parasite, lives on or in the other, the host. The parasite either harms its host or lives at the expense of the host. What is a parasite? A living organism which lives on or in another organism (host) and derives nutrition directly from it. This implies that the parasite benefits and the host is harmed but usually not killed. Types of parasites According to their location in the host, parasites are either; ectoparasites or endoparasites. If a parasite lives on the surface of its host, it is called an ectoparasite (e.g., lice), whereas if the parasite lives in the host, it is an endoparasite (e.g., malaria). Endoparasites are of the following types: • Obligate parasites: they can't exist without being parasitic in their hosts. text: Endoparasites are of the following types: • Obligate parasites: they can't exist without being parasitic in their hosts. (e.g., malaria) • Facultative parasites: they can lead a free-living life or live a parasitic life according to environmental conditions. (e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis) • Accidental parasites: they are parasites that infect an unusual host by accident. E.g., Toxocara canis is a worm of the dog w hen accidentally infects human, it does not complete its whole life cycle (reproduction) as it would in its specific host (the dog). Some parasites live their entire adult lives within or on their hosts and may be called permanent parasites, whereas a temporary, or intermittent, parasite, such as a mosquito or bed bug, only feeds on the host and then leaves. Temporary parasites are often referred to as micro-predators, in recognition of the fact that they usually “prey” on several different hosts (or the same host at several discrete times). What is a host? An organism that harbors the parasite and provides nourishment and shelter.

text: Temporary parasites are often referred to as micro-predators, in recognition of the fact that they usually “prey” on several different hosts (or the same host at several discrete times). What is a host? An organism that harbors the parasite and provides nourishment and shelter. Page 3 of 6 Types of hosts • Definitive host: is the host in which the parasite replicates sexually, or the adult stage of parasite (helminth) is present. • Intermediate host: is the host required by the parasite to complete the asexual stage of its life cycle and the larval stage of the parasite is present in it, e.g., the beef is the intermediate host for Taenia saginata (larvae develop in it), whereas, human is the definitive host for that helminth (adults develop in it). • Vector: the term vector is applied usually to arthropods which transmit parasites from one host to another. Effects of parasite on the host 1. Utilization of the host’s food Diphyllobothrium latum in man has been known to cause anemia like pernicious anemia, because of the affinity this tapeworm has for Vitamin B12. This tapeworm can absorb 10 -50 times as much vitamin B12 as other tapeworms. 2.

This tapeworm can absorb 10 -50 times as much vitamin B12 as other tapeworms. 2. Utilization of host’s non-nutritional materials. In some blood-feeding parasitic hookworms (e.g., Ancylostoma duodenale), the haemoglobin may drop 30% below normal. 3. Damage to host’s tissue. The parasites destroy the host’s tissue in two ways: (a) Some parasites destroy (injure) the host’s tissue when they enter the host. The cercariae of certain schistosomes that cause “Swimmer’s Itch” while penetrating the host skin cause inflammation and damage to the surrounding host tissues. (b) Others inflict tissue damage after they have successfully entered. Entamoeba histolytica which causes a moebic dysentery, secrets histolytic enzymes that digest the epithelial cells lining the host’s large intestine, causing ulcerations. 4. Abnormal growth.

Specific toxins or poisons, egested, secreted, or excreted by parasites are considered causes of irritation and damage to hosts. • An example of a parasite that elicits an allergic reaction in the host is Schistosoma cercaria which causes a severe inflammatory reaction leading to what is called cercarial dermatitis. • In case of blood-sucking insects such as mosquitoes, the reaction resulting from the bites represents the host’s response to the irritating salivary secretions of the insect. 6. Mechanical interference. Mechanical damage by nematode is also demonstrated by Ascaris lumbricoides in the intestine of their host.

Mechanical interference. Mechanical damage by nematode is also demonstrated by Ascaris lumbricoides in the intestine of their host. This intestinal parasite which measures up to 50 cm in length, when present in large numbers, can disturb intestinal motility leading to volvulus and intestinal obstruction. 7. Host-tissue reaction. Another example of host -tissue reaction is demonstrated by Trichinella spiralis encystment in mammalian muscles. Once the nematode larvae reach the musculature, it is surrounded by connective tissue cells and eosinophils. These host cells soon form a capsule around the coiled worm (larvae) hence the cyst is completely of host origin. Parasite Life Cycles. The life cycle of a parasite is the cycle of its development from the definitive host back to the same or another definitive host. It is termed a direct life cycle when a parasite requires only one specific species of the host in which it completes its development.

text: Page 1 of 12 L 17 What are Helminths? What are Protozoa? SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Classify medically important parasites 2. Define the terms related parasitic helminths and protozoa 3. Differentiate between different helminths and protozoa 4. Different elements of the life cycle Medical parasitology traditionally has included the study of three major groups of animals: parasitic helminths (worms), parasitic protozoa and those arthropods that directly cause disease or act as vectors of various pathogens. Medical Helminthology The term helminth is derived from the Greek language meaning worm. The helminths are multicellular, bilaterally symmetrical parasites having three germ layers – ectoderm, mesoderm, and entoderm. Helminths have the following characters: • The outer covering, known as cuticle, is tough. It is resistant to intestinal digestion and may be armed with spines or hooks. • Digestive and nervous systems are underdeveloped, whereas their reproductive system is well developed. The parasites may be hermaphrodite or have separate sexes.

The parasites may be hermaphrodite or have separate sexes. They also produce eggs in great number to help them survive. • Since they do not possess definite organs of locomotion, they generally move by muscular contraction and relaxation. Classification of Helminthes The helminths of medical importance are classified into two phylums: 1. Phylum Platyhelminthes (Flat worms) They have a dorso-ventrally flattened body, which is either leaf -shaped (Trematoda) or tape-shaped (Cestoda). 2. All trematodes possess at least two suckers as organs of attachment. Depending on their habitat they feed on blood, intestinal contents, biliary secreti ons, or tissue juices.

Page 1 of 4 18 General overview of arthropods SLOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to 1. Determine the general morphological characteristics of arthropods. 2. List the different types of arthropod development. 3. Identify arthropods’ relation to diseases. 4. List different methods by which arthropods can transfer organisms to man. 1. Introduction Arthropods are invertebrates in the phylum Arthropoda which are characterized by being bilaterally symmetrical, with external skeletons, and jointed appendages. The word “arthropod” is derived from the Greek arthron which means “joint” and podos which means “foot” or “leg” and together it means “jointed leg” . The exoskeleton or cuticle mainly consists of chitin, a polymer of glucosamine. The growth is accomplished through a series of molts because of the presence of this tough cuticle which protects the internal organs. They possess a complete digestive tract with the mouth and salivary glands and a complete digestive tract with an anus. After fertilization, females deposit eggs or larvae. Classification of Arthropods: Arthropods of medical importance are classified into the following classes: I. Class Crustacea e.g. cyclops. II. Class Arachnida e.g. scorpions, spiders, ticks and mites. III. Class Insecta or Hexapoda e.g. fleas, lice, bugs, mosquitoes and flies. General morphological criteria of arthropods: Identification of arthropods is essential to measure the risk of potential human threats. Arthropods are so diverse in their morphology; however, a brief description is listed below: I- Crustacea - Body formed of fused cephalothorax and segmented abdomen. - 5 pairs of legs. - 2 pairs of antennae. - No wings Ex: Cyclops II- Arachnida - Body formed of fused cephalothorax and segmented abdomen or fused together without any segmentation. Page 2 of 4 - 4 pairs of legs. - No antennae. Ex: Scorpion, ticks, and mites. III- Insecta - Body is segmented into head, thorax and abdomen. - 3 pairs of legs. - One pair of antennae.

III- Insecta - Body is segmented into head, thorax and abdomen. - 3 pairs of legs. - One pair of antennae. - Winged or not Ex: Fleas, lice, bugs, mosquitoes, and flies. Two different types of development take place (Figure. 1): 1 - Incomplete Metamorphosis: In this type of development, newly hatched larvae resemble adults but are smaller in size and sexually immature. Then they steadily increase in size through successive moltings, such as scorpions, ticks, mites, bugs, and lice. 2- Complete Metamorphosis: The newly hatched larvae are morphologically distinct from the adults. They may be worm-like and develop into the inactive pupal stage from which adults emerge, such as fleas, flies, and mosquitoes. Figure. 1: a. Incomplete metamorphosis (ticks), b. Complete metamorphosis (flies) Arthropods and their relation to disease Medically important arthropods are agents transmitting and /or causing diseases to man. I. Arthropods as Vectors of Pathogens (Disease Transmitters): They might act as mechanical vectors of the etiologic agent or as biological vectors that play an important part in the life cycle. 1.

Arthropods as Vectors of Pathogens (Disease Transmitters): They might act as mechanical vectors of the etiologic agent or as biological vectors that play an important part in the life cycle. 1. Mechanical Transmission When the arthropods transport the various pathogens in or on their bodies (their legs, hairs and antennae) and drop them unchanged on human food, drink or tissues, for example, the role of house fly in the transmission of enteric pathogens such as polio a b Page 3 of 4 virus and cholera, cysts of protozoa and eggs of helminths. 2. Biological Transmission This method of transmission occurs when the arthropod actively participates in the transmission of the organism. This type of transmission can be divided into: a. Propagative: The organism only multiplies in the arthropod without any cyclical development like in a culture tube, such as the multiplication of Yersinia pestis (causing plague) in fleas. b. Cyclodevelopmental: The organism undergoes developmental or morphological changes only without multiplication in the arthropod, such as the development of microfilaria of filarial worms within the mosquitoes. c.

Cyclodevelopmental: The organism undergoes developmental or morphological changes only without multiplication in the arthropod, such as the development of microfilaria of filarial worms within the mosquitoes. c. Cyclopropagative: The organism undergoes both developmental changes and multiplication in the arthropod, e.g. Plasmodia in the female Anopheles mosquito and Leishmania species in sand fly. Arthropods can transfer the organisms to man by different methods: 1. Salivary Secretion: Pathogens are discharged in minute droplets with the salivary secretion at when the arthropod is taking a blood meal, e.g., Plasmodia by female Anopheles mosquitoes. 2. Vomit -drop: Non-blood-sucking flies (e.g., house flies) may deposit pathogen-containing vomit drops on human food or drink, such as Entamoeba histolytica cysts. On the other hand, blood-sucking arthropods may obtain the pathogenic organisms in a blood meal from an infected person and deposit them in vomit drops in the puncture wound made in the skin of an uninfected person, e.g., Leishmania species by sandflies and Yersinia pestis causing the plague by fleas. 3. Faeces: Non-blood-sucking flies (e.g., house flies) may deposit their pathogen-containing faeces on human food or drink, such as Entamoeba histolytica cysts. 4. Arthropods as Etiological Agents of Disease (Causing Disease) In addition to their importance in the transmission of pathogens to man, arthropods themselves play a significant role as disease-producing agents. 1. Toxins and venoms: introduced into the skin by tick bites or scorpion stings cause local and/or systemic reactions. 2. Allergic reactions: These reactions may occur due to the injection of the saliva of blood- sucking arthropods into the skin of the host, e.g., dermatitis caused by the bites of female mosquitoes and fleas. In addition, house dust mites may cause rhinitis or asthma by serving directly as allergens or by concentrating highly antigenic material. However, the degree of reaction can vary remarkably between individuals, from little or no reaction to quite severe dermal and systemic effects which may require medical attention. 3. Specific diseases: Certain arthropods produce lesions in humans through their presence in Page 4 of 4 the tissues (the adult or any developmental stage), for example, the presence of larvae of higher diptera in the tissues causing myiasis and the presence of itch mites in skin tissue causing scabies.

The sting may cause redness and swelling along with a burning sensation. Scorpions sting to defend and protect themselves. Local effects: - immediate intense aching pain or burning sensation at the sting site - lymphadenitis - Redness, swelling, and warmth around the sting area - Numbness or tingling Systemic effects (in severe cases): - Sweating and salivation - Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain - Muscle twitching, spasms, or convulsions - glossopharyngeal involvement so that speech and swallowing become difficult, - Respiratory distress. - Tachycardia, hypertension, or hypotension - Neurological symptoms such as seizures, paralysis, or altered consciousness. Treatment You usually won’t need medical treatment for a sting. You can typically treat a sting at home with ice, elevation, pain medication, and antihistamines. • First aid measures: - Clean the sting site with soap and water. - Apply a cold compress to reduce pain and swelling. - Keep the affected limb elevated. • Pain management: - Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or acetaminophen may be used to alleviate pain. • Antivenom therapy: - Specific scorpion antivenom may be administered in severe cases of envenomation to neutralize the venom and prevent further toxicity. • Supportive care: - Maintain hydration with intravenous fluids. - Monitor vital signs and provide respiratory support if needed. - Treat complications such as allergic reactions, cardiac arrhythmias, or respiratory failure. Prevention Educate the patient on ways to prevent scorpion stings, such as avoiding areas where scorpions are commonly found, shaking out clothing and bedding before use, and using insecticides or professional pest control services if necessary. Control - Louse-infested clothing is subjected to a minimum temperature of 70 °C for at least an hour. - Insecticidal dusts, such as carbaryl, propoxur, malathion or permethrin applied to a person’s body. - Impregnation of clothing with a pyrethroid insecticide may provide long-lasting protection against louse infestations, and such treated clothing may remain effective after several washings. Definition Myiasis is a zoonosis derived from the Greek word (mya, or fly) . Myiasis is the infestation of live vertebrates (humans and/or animals) with larvae of medium -sized and large dipterous flies. These larvae (Maggots) can feed on the host's living or dead tissue, liquid body substance, or ingested food. Risk factors Myiasis in humans is distributed world wide but more common in tropics and sub-tropical regions. Low socioeconomic state and poor hygienic measures are main risk factors. Myiasis is considered an important Traveler-associated skin disease. Nosocomial infestations are not uncommon. Causative agent Larvae of flies (Maggots) are the causative agents of myiasis.

Introduction Diagnosis of parasitic infections can be achieved by: 1. History taking which includes travel history to endemic places, the patient's geographic location, history of exposure to contaminated water or arthropod bites, and family history. 2. Clinical diagnosis depends on the characteristic signs and symptoms related to the parasitic infection, such as diarrhea, dysentery, or blood in the stool or urine. 3. Laboratory diagnosis can be obtained by the following methods: • Direct methods: include macroscopic and microscopic examination of the patient’s samples. • Indirect methods: include immunological tests. • Molecular methods. Laboratory diagnosis can be obtained by the following methods: • Direct methods: include macroscopic and microscopic examination of the patient’s samples. • Indirect methods: include immunological tests. • Molecular methods. Laboratory diagnosis of parasitic infections I. Direct methods for diagnosis of parasitic infections: This is based on the examination of excreta, body fluids, and tissues and the visualization of the different diagnostic stages of parasites. The samples examined could be one of the following: stool, urine, aspirates, sputum, biopsy, and blood. A. Stool Examination: It aids in the identification of parasite infections of the small and large intestines, as well as the biliary tract. Samples should be collected in a wide- mouthed container with a screw top. The sample should not be contaminated with urine or water because urine can kill some parasites and water can contain ciliates, which can lead to false diagnosis. It is also important to ensure that the patient is not receiving antibiotics or has had a barium enema, as both will hide any parasitic infection. Three stool samples should be examined as one sample every other day. 1. Macroscopic Examination a.

It is also important to ensure that the patient is not receiving antibiotics or has had a barium enema, as both will hide any parasitic infection. Three stool samples should be examined as one sample every other day. 1. Macroscopic Examination a. The consistency should be noted whether formed, semi-formed, or liquid, since trophic forms of protozoa are found in liquid or diarrheic stools, while cystic forms are found more in the formed and semi-formed samples. b. The composition of the sample is also important whether there is blood and/or mucus a Page 2 of 18 such as in dysentery. c. The colour is pale as in steatorrhoeic conditions, e.g., Giardia lamblia infection. It can also be black or red in colour when iron is taken or when there is intestinal haemorrhage. d. Microscopic Examination a. Direct Saline Smear: It is prepared by mixing a small portion of stool with a drop of normal saline. It is most useful for the detection of motility of protozoa, e.g., Trophozoites of amoeba and Giardia lamblia, if the stool sample is examined within one hour after discharge (Figure 2). Helminthic eggs may also be seen if they are present in large numbers (Figures 3-5). Iodine Smear In this method stool samples are emulsified in 1% iodine solution. The iodine stains the cysts of protozoa revealing their details (Figure 6). Its main disadvantage is that the trophozoites are rapidly killed by the iodine and therefore become non-motile. Figure 6: Protozoan Cyst Stained with Iodine (Giardia lamblia) Direct saline smear and iodine smear are useful only when helminth eggs and protozoa are in large numbers. If they are scarce or scanty then concentration techniques are required. The concentration methods fall into two general categories: sedimentation and floatation methods. Page 5 of 18 c. Concentration Techniques i. Sedimentation Methods Principle: Most helminthic eggs and protozoal cysts are heavier than the suspending liquid and so they sink and concentrate at the bottom of the tube i.e sediment, which is taken and examined.

The ether adsorbs the faecal debris which becomes lighter than water and floats to the top, while the addition of formalin fixes and preserves the specimens. Figure 7: Formol Ether Concentration Technique. ii. Floatation Method Principle: This involves the use of solutions that have a higher specific gravity than the organisms to be floated so that the organisms rise to the top and the debris sinks to the bottom giving a cleaner preparation. The floatation procedure permits the separation of protozoan cysts and eggs of some helminths by using concentrated saline or zinc sulphate solution. The main disadvantage is that heavy eggs and operculated eggs do not concentrate well with this technique. d. Estimation of the intensity of infection of schistosomes as a test of cure after treatment is also important. • Kato Katz Technique (Figure 11) In this technique a portion of a sieved stool sample is transferred to a hole of a template on a slide. After filling the hole, the template is removed, and the sample is covered with a piece of cellophane soaked in glycerine to clear the fecal material from around the eggs. The eggs, e.g., Schistosoma eggs, are then counted and the egg number per gram of faeces is calculated. Page 8 of 18 Figure 11: Kato Katz Technique ii. NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 10 21 HEPATITIS VIRUSES (B, D) ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Analyze the molecular biology and structural characteristics of HBV and HDV to explain their replication cycles and mechanisms of therapeutic resistance. 2. Differentiate between the immunopathological mechanisms driving acute liver injury, extrahepatic immune-complex manifestations, and age-dependent chronicity in viral hepatitis. 3. Interpret complex virologic and serologic profiles to classify chronic hepatitis B infection phases (Phases 1–4, occult infection, window period) and guide clinical disease management. 4. Formulate appropriate evidence-based strategies for treatment, pre-exposure vaccination, and post-exposure prophylaxis for HBV and HDV in diverse clinical scenarios. HEPATITIS B VIRUS Structure - HBV is the major member of the hepadnaviruses. Other members of this family include woodchuck, ground squirrel, and duck hepatitis viruses. HBV infects the liver and, to a lesser extent, the kidneys and pancreas of only humans and chimpanzees. - HBV is a small enveloped DNA virus.

Other members of this family include woodchuck, ground squirrel, and duck hepatitis viruses. HBV infects the liver and, to a lesser extent, the kidneys and pancreas of only humans and chimpanzees. - HBV is a small enveloped DNA virus. Specifically, the genome is a small, circular, partly double-stranded DNA. Although a DNA virus, it encodes a reverse transcriptase and replicates through an RNA intermediate. - The virion, also called the Dane particle, is 42 nm in diameter. The virions are unusually stable for an enveloped virus. They resist treatment with ether, low pH, freezing, and moderate heating. These characteristics assist transmission from one person to another and hamper disinfection. - The viral genome encodes four overlapping open reading frames (ORFs), C, P , S, and X, from which funcQonal viral proteins are produced: o Hepatitis B Core antigen HBc and its relatives such as E antigen (HBe); HBc: viral capsid protein which is only present inside hepatocytes and detected in liver biopsies and not detected in serum. Which of these occurs seems to be determined by the person’s immune response to the infection. The major source of infectious virus is blood, but HBV can be found in semen, saliva, milk, vaginal secretions, and amniotic fluid.

The major source of infectious virus is blood, but HBV can be found in semen, saliva, milk, vaginal secretions, and amniotic fluid. The most efficient way to acquire HBV is through: (1) injection of the virus into the bloodstream [Per-cutaneous transmission including intramuscular, intravenous, NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 3 of 10 subcutaneous or intra-dermal injections, tattooing, ear piercing and needle stick. Contamination of skin lesions (fresh cutaneous scratch, abrasion and burns). Infected blood and blood products through transfusion or dialysis. (2) Common but less efficient routes of infection are sexual contact and birth (Perinatal transmission when mothers are HBsAg positive due to leak of maternal blood to infant’s circulation during birth. Transplacental transmission is rare). The virus starts to replicate in hepatocytes of the liver within 3 days of its acquisition, with minimal cytopathic effect. Symptoms may not be observed for 45 days or longer because they are primarily caused by immunopathology.

The virus starts to replicate in hepatocytes of the liver within 3 days of its acquisition, with minimal cytopathic effect. Symptoms may not be observed for 45 days or longer because they are primarily caused by immunopathology. The infectious dose, the route of infection, and the person determine the incubation period. Infection proceeds for a relatively long time without causing liver damage (i.e., elevation of liver enzyme levels) or symptoms. Copies of the HBV genome integrate into the hepatocyte DNA and can remain latent. HBsAg particles continue to be released into the blood even after virion release has ended and until the infection is resolved. An individual is infectious when both the HBsAg and the HBeAg components of the virion can be detected in the blood. Cell-mediated immunity and inflammation are responsible for causing the symptoms and effecting resolution of the HBV infection by eliminating the infected hepatocyte. An insufficient T-cell response to the infection generally results in the occurrence of mild symptoms, an inability to resolve the infection, and development of chronic hepatitis.

An insufficient T-cell response to the infection generally results in the occurrence of mild symptoms, an inability to resolve the infection, and development of chronic hepatitis. Chronic infection also exhausts CD8 T cells, preventing them from killing infected cells. Infants and young children have an immature cell- mediated immune response and are less able to resolve the infection, but they suffer less tissue damage and milder symptoms. As many as 90% of infants infected perinatally become chronic carriers. Viral replication persists in these people for long periods. Antibodies can protect against initial infection by preventing delivery of the virus to the liver. Later in the infection, the large amount of HBsAg in serum binds to and blocks the action of neutralizing antibody, which limits the antibody’s ability to resolve an infection. Immune complexes formed between HBsAg and anti-HBs contribute to the development of hypersensitivity reactions (type III), leading to problems such as vasculitis, arthralgia, rash, and renal damage. Antibodies to HBc and HBe are present in serum but are nonprotective.

Antibodies to HBc and HBe are present in serum but are nonprotective. The HBeAg protein, like HBsAg, is released into serum, and during its production, anti-HBe is bound to the antigen and undetectable. The HBc antigen is present in cells or virions and inaccessible to the antibody in blood. As a result, anti-HBc is detectable upon production, throughout and after the course of the infection. Genetic variability of HBV: The lack of reverse transcriptase proofreading activity leads to frequent mutations of the viral genome. This results in the coexistence of genetically distinct viral species in infected individuals, also called viral quasispecies, which evolve depending on the pressure from the host environment. The interplay between the virus, hepatocyte and the immune response or antiviral treatment is thought to drive the emergence of HBV mutants that have the capacity to escape immune responses or antiviral treatments.

NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 1 of 5 1 BASIC CONCEPTS OF INFECTION ILOs By the end of this lecture, students will be able to: 1. Explain the cellular and biological characteristics that distinguish major groups of medically important microorganisms and relate them to their clinical significance. 2. Differentiate resident, transient, and potentially pathogenic microbiota in relation to colonization and disease. 3. Analyze the microbiota of different body sites to distinguish normal colonization from findings suggestive of infection. 4. Apply the principles of colonization resistance, dysbiosis, and opportunistic infection to clinical situations involving disruption of normal microbiota or host barriers. MICROBIAL WORLD The spectrum of infection has widened, with discoveries that organisms earlier thought to be harmless can cause disease under certain circumstances. Who could have guessed that Helicobacter pylori, would be the major cause of gastric and duodenal ulcers and an officially declared carcinogen?

MICROBIAL WORLD The spectrum of infection has widened, with discoveries that organisms earlier thought to be harmless can cause disease under certain circumstances. Who could have guessed that Helicobacter pylori, would be the major cause of gastric and duodenal ulcers and an officially declared carcinogen? Moreover, bioterrorist forces have unearthed two previously controlled infectious diseases—anthrax and smallpox—and threatened their distribution as agents of biological warfare. For students of medicine, understanding the fundamental basis of infectious diseases has more relevance than ever. The science of medical microbiology dates back to the pioneering studies of Pasteur and Koch, who isolated specific agents and proved that they could cause disease by introducing the experimental method. Microbiology is the study of all living organisms that are too small to be visible with the naked eye. This includes bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, prions, protozoa and algae, collectively known as 'microbes'. These microbes play key roles in nutrient cycling, biodegradation/biodeterioration, climate change, food spoilage, the cause and control of disease, and biotechnology.

This includes bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, prions, protozoa and algae, collectively known as 'microbes'. These microbes play key roles in nutrient cycling, biodegradation/biodeterioration, climate change, food spoilage, the cause and control of disease, and biotechnology. The major classes of microorganisms in terms of ascending size and complexity are prions, viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites. All organisms other than viruses and prions are made up of cells. Although viruses have genetic material (DNA or RNA) they are not cellular, lacking cell membranes, cytoplasm and the machinery for synthesizing macromolecules, depending instead upon host cells for this process. The agents (prions) lack nucleic acid and consist only of infectious proteinaceous particles. All other organisms have a cellular organization, being made up of single cells (most ‘microbes’) or of many cells. Each cell has genetic material (DNA) and cytoplasm with synthetic machinery, and is bounded by a cell membrane. Bacteria are prokaryotes; all other organisms are eukaryotes. In fact, from shortly after birth on, it is universal; Current estimates indicate that the numbers of microbial and human cells are of the same order of magnitude, with an approximate ratio close to 1:1. This population formerly called the normal flora is now referred to as our microbiota or microbiome. These microorganisms, which are overwhelmingly bacteria, are frequently found colonizing various body sites in healthy individuals. The constituents and numbers of the microbiota vary in different areas of the body and, sometimes, at different ages and physiologic states. Thus, each accessible area of the body presents a particular ecologic niche, colonization of which requires a particular set of properties of the colonizing microbe. Meheissen Page 3 of 5 Organisms of the microbiota may have a symbiotic relationship that benefits the host or may simply live as commensals with a neutral relationship to the host. The members of the human microbiota may stay for highly variable periods; 1) Residents are strains that have an established niche at one of the many body sites, which they occupy indefinitely.

The members of the human microbiota may stay for highly variable periods; 1) Residents are strains that have an established niche at one of the many body sites, which they occupy indefinitely. 2)Transients are acquired from the environment and establish themselves briefly, but they tend to be excluded by competition from residents or by the host’s innate or immune defense mechanisms. The term carrier state is used when organisms known to be potentially pathogenic are involved, although its implication of risk is not always justified. For example, Streptococcus pneumoniae, a cause of pneumonia, and Neisseria meningitidis, a cause of meningitis, may be isolated from the throat of 5% to 40% of healthy people. Whether these bacteria represent transient flora, resident flora, or carrier state is largely semantic. It is important to understand the role of the microbiota because of its significance both as a defense mechanism against infection and as a source of potentially pathogenic organisms. In addition, it is important for physicians to know the typical composition of the microbiota at various sites to avoid confusion when interpreting laboratory culture results.

Microbiota at different body sites 1. Blood, Body Fluids, and Tissues In health, the blood, body fluids, and tissues are sterile. Occasional organisms may be displaced across epithelial barriers as a result of trauma or during childbirth; they may be briefly recoverable from the bloodstream before they are filtered out in the pulmonary capillaries or removed by cells of the reticuloendothelial system. Such transient bacteremia may be the source of infection when structures such as damaged heart valves and foreign bodies (prostheses) are in the bloodstream. 2. Skin The skin surface provides a dry, slightly acidic, aerobic environment. It plays host to an abundant flora that varies according to the presence of its appendages (hair, nails) and the activity of sebaceous and sweat glands. The flora is more abundant on moist skin areas (axillae, perineum, and between toes). e.g. Staphylococci, Propionibacterium, and diphtheroids. Even with antiseptic scrubbing, it is difficult to eliminate bacteria from skin sites, particularly those bearing pilosebaceous units. Organisms of the skin flora are resistant to the bactericidal effects of skin lipids and fatty acids, which inhibit or kill many extraneous bacteria. 3. Gastrointestinal tract The mouth and pharynx contain large numbers of facultative and anaerobic bacteria. The stomach contains few, if any, resident organisms in health because of the lethal action of gastric hydrochloric acid and peptic enzymes on bacteria.

HEPATITIS C VIRUS Structure & Replication - HCV is the only member of the Hepacivirus genus of the Flaviviridae family. - HCV has a positive-sense RNA genome, and is enveloped. - The genome encodes 10 proteins, including 3 structural [one core protein and two glycoproteins (E1, E2)] as well as 7 non-structural proteins. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is error prone and generates mutations in the glycoprotein and other genes. This generates antigenic variability. Such variability makes development of a vaccine very difficult. - There are seven major genotypes (1-7) of HCV (clades), and between and within each genotype there is considerable genetic and antigenic diversity. Different genotypes predominate in different parts of the world. Genotype 4a is the most common in Egypt. HCV Genetic diversity is not correlated with differences in clinical disease, although differences exist in response to antiviral therapy. Figure 1.

Structure and genome organization of HCV NMD3101 Principles of Infection Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Page 2 of 10 Pathogenesis & Immunity - HCV is transmitted primarily in infected blood and sexually. Intravenous drug abusers and tattoo recipients are at highest risk to HCV infection. Screening procedures have led to a reduction in the levels of transmission by blood transfusion and organ donation. Almost all (>90%) HIV-infected people who are or were intravenous drug users are infected with HCV. - The high incidence of chronic asymptomatic infections promotes the spread of the virus in the population. - The ability of HCV to remain cell associated and prevent host cell death promotes persistent infection but results in liver disease later in life. - The virus’s ability to evade interferon action and change its antigenicity help the virus establish chronic disease. - Cell-mediated immune responses are necessary to resolve the infection but also cause tissue damage.

text: - The virus’s ability to evade interferon action and change its antigenicity help the virus establish chronic disease. - Cell-mediated immune responses are necessary to resolve the infection but also cause tissue damage. - Antibody to HCV is not protective. Due to the selective pressure from the host, and the antigenic variations that occur in the E2/E1 proteins, the virus evade the humoral immune response and establish a persistent infection. - HCV antibodies have also been implicated in the formation of immune complexes against the liver and other tissues. During acute infection, the rise in serum transaminases is due to immune-mediated hepatocyte damage. The immune complexes are also deposited in other tissues and cause extrahepatic complications, including vasculitis, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, and others. - Chronic HCV infection results in inflammatory response that may lead to progressive fibrosis and hepatocarcinogenesis. - The chronic infection can exhaust CD8 cytotoxic T cells so they cannot resolve the infection. text: - Chronic HCV infection results in inflammatory response that may lead to progressive fibrosis and hepatocarcinogenesis. - The chronic infection can exhaust CD8 cytotoxic T cells so they cannot resolve the infection. Clinical syndromes - A viremia can be detected within 1 to 3 weeks of infection. The viremia lasts 4 to 6 months in people with an acute infection and longer than 10 years in those with a persistent infection. - The incubation period ranges from 2 weeks to 6 months. - HCV has the highest rate of chronicity (> 75%). - More commonly (>70% of cases), the initial disease is asymptomatic or clinically mild (20–30% have jaundice; 10–20% have only nonspecific symptoms such as anorexia, malaise, and abdominal pain) but establishes chronic persistent disease. The predominant symptom is chronic fatigue. Chronic persistent disease often progresses to chronic active hepatitis within 10 to 15 years and to cirrhosis (20% of chronic cases) and liver failure (20% of cirrhotic cases) after 20 years. HCV promotes the development of hepatocellular carcinoma after 30 years in up to 5% of chronically infected patients.

Nucleic acid-based assays (eg, RT- PCR) detect the presence of circulating HCV RNA and are useful for diagnosis of acute infection soon after exposure and for monitoring patients on antiviral therapy (Confirm sustained virologic response (SVR) following treatment). Nucleic acid assays also are used to genotype HCV isolates. 2. Serologic assays are available for diagnosis of HCV infection. Seroconversion occurs within 3-6 months of infection. Antibodies are directed against core, and NS3, NS4 and NS5 proteins and tend to be relatively low in titer. Serological assays include: enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), chemiluminescence immunoassay (CIA) and point of care immunoassay tests employing multiple HCV antigens. text: Direct microscopic examination Microscopic examination of stained or unstained specimens is a relatively simple and inexpensive, but much less sensitive method than culture for detection of small numbers of bacteria. A specimen must contain at least 10 5 organisms per milliliter before it is likely that organisms will be seen on a smear. Gram stain (all bacteria) ZN stain (mycobacteria) Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) staining Gram staining is a very useful procedure in diagnostic microbiology. Most specimens submitted when bacterial infection is suspected should be smeared on glass slides, Gram-stained, and examined microscopically. On microscopic examination of any specimen (Direct Smear) the Gram reaction (purple indicates Gram-positive organisms; red indicates Gram-negative) morphology (shape: cocci, rods, fusiform, or other) of bacteria should be noted. the presence or absence of inflammatory cells and the type of cell are important to note and quantify. The appearance of bacteria on Gram-stained smears does not permit identification of species . 1.

text: Culture and Identification The standard medium for specimens is blood agar , usually made with 5% sheep blood. Most aerobic and facultatively anaerobic organisms will grow on blood agar. Chocolate agar , a medium containing heated blood with or without supplements, is a second necessary medium; some organisms that do not grow on blood agar, including pathogenic Neisseria and Haemophilus , will grow on chocolate agar. A selective medium for enteric Gram-negative rods ( MacConkey agar ) is a third type of medium used routinely. These agars contain indicators that allow differentiation of lactose- fermenting organisms from non-lactose-fermenting organisms. Specimens to be cultured for obligate anaerobes must be plated on anaerobic media . Routine culture media 2. Culture and Identification S elective culture media Many other specialized media ( selective media ) are used in diagnostic bacteriology; choices depend on the clinical diagnosis and the organism under consideration upon physician request . The laboratory staff selects the specific media on the basis of the information in the culture request.

text: Culture and Identification S elective culture media Many other specialized media ( selective media ) are used in diagnostic bacteriology; choices depend on the clinical diagnosis and the organism under consideration upon physician request . The laboratory staff selects the specific media on the basis of the information in the culture request. For culture of mycobacteria , specialized media ( Lowenstein Jensen ) are commonly used. These media may contain inhibitors of other bacteria. Because many mycobacteria grow slowly, the cultures must be incubated and examined periodically for weeks . In addition to the above standard and selective media, agars that incorporate antibiotics and chromogenic enzyme substrates that impart color to specific organisms of interest, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus are available. These media, while more expensive, do enhance sensitivity by inhibiting background microbiota and allowing the pathogen of interest to be more easily recognized. Typically, these chromogenic agars are used for specimens such as surveillance cultures . Chromogenic c ulture media 2.

Molecular assays Nucleic acid–based methods are generally specific and highly sensitive and can be used for all categories of microbes . Results can be provided rapidly . Because each test typically is specific to a single organism, the clinician must know the diagnostic possibilities and request tests accordingly. Recent advances have led to the development of multiplex assays , in which a single nucleic acid–based test can detect and differentiate between ≥ 2 causative microorganisms. Multiplex assays have similar sensitivity and specificity as single target assays . 4. Serological testing Detection of specific antibodies to infectious agents can be useful for diagnosis of acute or chronic infections, and for investigating the epidemiology of infectious disease. During the course of illness, IgM antibody is first produced, followed by appearance of IgG antibody. Serology is most useful when acute and convalescent sera are tested to show increases in antibody titers over time. There are a variety of serological assays available, including direct immunofluorescence, agglutination, EIA, and ELISA. 6. text: Mass spectrometry Mass spectrometry (MS), a technology used to analyze proteins , has revolutionized the approach to microbial identification in clinical laboratories. MS employs methods such as ionization radiation to disrupt material, forming charged particles that are identified in various ways on the basis of mass or mass-to-charge ratio. M atrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of- flight mass spectroscopy ( MALDI-TOF MS) . MALDI-TOF allows identif ication of bacteria and yeast isolates recovered in clinical cultures. The assays involve making a thin smear from a colony or broth culture onto a metallic slide of the organism to be identified and applying an acid matrix to it. The slide is placed into the instrument where the organism mixture is hit by laser pulses. Charged protein fragments are produced and accelerated through an electrostatic field in a vacuum tube until they contact the mass spectrometer’s detector. Molecules of different masses and charges “fly” at different speeds (“time of flight”).

Appraise the antibiogram according to clinical condition of the patient Introduction Deciding whether any bacterium should be considered susceptible or resistant to an antimicrobial involves an integrated assessment of: (1) in vitro activity by antimicrobial susceptibility test, (2) pharmacologic characteristics of the antibiotic (dosage, routes, frequency of administration, absorption, metabolism, excretion), (3) clinical factors of the patient.

text: Appraise the antibiogram according to clinical condition of the patient Introduction Deciding whether any bacterium should be considered susceptible or resistant to an antimicrobial involves an integrated assessment of: (1) in vitro activity by antimicrobial susceptibility test, (2) pharmacologic characteristics of the antibiotic (dosage, routes, frequency of administration, absorption, metabolism, excretion), (3) clinical factors of the patient. Any agent approved for clinical use has demonstrated in vitro its potential to inhibit the growth of some target group of bacteria at concentrations that can be achieved with acceptable risks of toxicity ; that is, the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Thus, MIC is defined as the least amount of antimicrobial that will inhibit growth of an organism. In selecting therapy , clinicians must consider more than the results of laboratory tests . The clinical pharmacology of the drug, the cause of the disease, the site of infection, the immune function of the patient, the pathology of the lesion must be taken into account as well. For example, the antimicrobial must reach the subarachnoid space and cerebrospinal fluid in meningitis.

text: Dilution tests D etermine the MIC directly by using serial dilutions of the antimicrobial agent . The dilutions are prepared in tubes or microdilution wells , concentrations are doubled using a base of 1 μg /mL (0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on). The bacterial inoculum is adjusted to a standard ( 10 5 to 10 6 bacteria/mL ) and added to the broth. After incubation, the tubes are examined for turbidity produced by bacterial growth. B roth microdilution method The first tube in which visible growth is absent (clear) is the MIC for that organism. Guidelines available from CLSI provide interpretive criteria, defining strains as resistant, intermediate, or susceptible to a certain drug based on the MIC. Bactericidal effects can be estimated by subculturing the clear broth from MIC testing onto antibiotic-free solid media . 3. Automated tests Instruments are now available that carry out rapid, automated variants of the broth dilution test . In these systems the bacteria are incubated with the antimicrobial in specialized modules that are read automatically on a frequent basis.

The multiple readings and the increased sensitivity of determining endpoints by turbidimetric or fluorometric analysis makes it possible to generate MICs in as little as 4 hours . In laboratories with sufficient volume, these methods are no more expensive than manual methods, and the rapid results have enhanced potential to influence clinical outcome , particularly when interfaced with computerized hospital information systems. However, they often involve specialized equipment and demand professional interpretation. PCR, DNA microarray, whole-genome sequencing, and metagenomics are examples of such practices. Among molecular diagnostic techniques, PCR is a highly recognized detection tool.

The plan emphasized the importance and need of “ effective, fast, and low-cost diagnostic technologies for guiding the appropriate use of antibiotics .” This action plan aims to improve the speed and accuracy of diagnosis through quick, accurate, and minimal cost point-of-care testing (POCT) diagnostic technologies . Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg MED217 Principles of infection Tutorial 2 2. Antigen detection Commercial kits are available to detect many viruses . Multiple types of assays are used as well: EIA, IF , latex agglutination, Immunochromatography, etc. In general, the antigen detection assays for viruses are less sensitive than the viral culture methods and NAATs . M any of these assays have been replaced by NAATs 3. Nucleic acid amplification techniques A wide variety of commercial assays are available to detect viral nucleic acid or to amplify and detect it. These procedures are rapidly becoming the standards for diagnostic virology , supplanting the traditional virus culture and antigen detection techniques. The methods include PCR, reverse transcriptase PCR, others. The procedures allow detection as well as quantitation of the viruses . Data from quantitative assays are used to guide antiviral therapy in multiple viral diseases. E.g. RT-PCR for HCV.

text: Indirect ELISA Indirect IF Immunoblot technique Western blot is used to identify an antigen in a complex mixture of proteins . The complex mixture of proteins is subjected to gel electrophoresis (PAGE). This separates the proteins according to charge and molecular size. The gel is then blotted to a nitrocellulose membrane. The membrane is incubated with a serum sample. If the serum contains specific antibody that reacts with a protein on the membrane, the immobilized proteins capture virus-specific antibody and are visualized with an enzyme-conjugated antihuman antibody. text: BASIC CONCEPTS OF INFECTION Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 1 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize the importance of medical microbiology Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Understand the definition of medical microbiology. 2. Recognize the types of human microbiota. 3. Differentiate between resident and transient microbiota. 4. Relate the role of microbiota in different body sites with health and disease. • The spectrum of infection has widened , with discoveries that organisms earlier thought to be harmless can cause disease under certain circumstances. • Who could have guessed that Helicobacter pylori, would be the major cause of gastric and duodenal ulcers and an officially declared carcinogen? • Moreover, bioterrorist forces have unearthed two previously controlled infectious diseases —anthrax and smallpox—and threatened their distribution as agents of biological warfare.

• Moreover, bioterrorist forces have unearthed two previously controlled infectious diseases —anthrax and smallpox—and threatened their distribution as agents of biological warfare. • For students of medicine, understanding the fundamental basis of infectious diseases has more relevance than ever. • The science of medical microbiology dates back to the pioneering studies of Pasteur and Koch , who isolated specific agents and proved that they could cause disease by introducing the experimental method. • Microbiology is the study of all living organisms that are too small to be visible with the naked eye. This includes bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, prions, protozoa and algae, collectively known as 'microbes’. • These microbes play key roles in nutrient cycling, biodegradation/biodeterioration, climate change, food spoilage, the cause and control of disease, and biotechnology. Classification of medically important microbes 13 • All organisms other than viruses and prions are made up of cells.

• These microbes play key roles in nutrient cycling, biodegradation/biodeterioration, climate change, food spoilage, the cause and control of disease, and biotechnology. Classification of medically important microbes 13 • All organisms other than viruses and prions are made up of cells. • Although viruses have genetic material (DNA or RNA) they are not cellular, lacking cell membranes, cytoplasm and the machinery for synthesizing macromolecules, depending instead upon host cells for this process. • The agents ( prions) lack nucleic acid and consist only of infectious proteinaceous particles. • All other organisms have a cellular organization, being made up of single cells (most ‘microbes’) or of many cells. Each cell has genetic material (DNA) and cytoplasm with synthetic machinery, and is bounded by a cell membrane. Bacteria are prokaryotes; all other organisms are eukaryotes. The major classes of microorganisms in terms of ascending size and complexity are prions, viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites.
