Eukaryotic cell Prokaryotic cell Cell size Large (10-100 µm) Small (0.5-5 µm) Organism type Multicellular Unicellular Nucleus Present (membrane bound) Absent (nucleoid region) Replication Mitotic division Binary fission Membrane bounds organelles e.g mitochondria Present Absent Ribosomes Large (80S) Small (70S) Cytoplasm Present Present Plasma membrane Present Present Cell wall Simple (present in fungi) Peptidoglycan (present in all prokaryotes) • Eukaryotes vs prokaryotes Human Microbiota • The presence of microbes on or in humans is not, by itself, abnormal. • Current estimates indicate that the numbers of microbial and human cells are of the same order of magnitude, with an approximate ratio close to 1:1. . • This population formerly called the normal flora is now referred to as our microbiota or microbiome. • These microorganisms, which are overwhelmingly bacteria, are frequently found colonizing various body sites in healthy individuals.

• This population formerly called the normal flora is now referred to as our microbiota or microbiome. • These microorganisms, which are overwhelmingly bacteria, are frequently found colonizing various body sites in healthy individuals. • The constituents and numbers of the microbiota vary in different areas of the body and, sometimes, at different ages and physiologic states. Thus, each accessible area of the body presents a particular ecologic niche, colonization of which requires a particular set of properties of the colonizing microbe. • Organisms of the microbiota may have a symbiotic relationship that benefits the host or • may simply live as commensals with a neutral relationship to the host. • The members of the human microbiota may stay for highly variable periods: 1) Residents are strains that have an established niche at one of the many body sites, which they occupy indefinitely. 2) Transients are acquired from the environment and establish themselves briefly, but they tend to be excluded by competition from residents or by the host’s innate or immune defense mechanisms.

Correlate bacterial growth curve with infectious disease course Bacterial size and shape • The small size (0.5 – 5 µm) • Nearly colorless nature of bacteria require the use of stains (Gram stain) for visualization with a light microscope. Hence, bacteria are generally referred to Gram positive (violet) and Gram negative (red). • The major morphologic forms are spheres, rods, bent or curved rods, and spirals. Spherical or oval bacteria are called cocci and are typically arranged in clusters or chains. Rods are called bacilli and may be straight or curved.

Rods are called bacilli and may be straight or curved. Bacilli that are small and pleomorphic to the point of resembling cocci are often called coccobacilli. Envelope and appendages • A rigid cell wall surrounds all bacterial cells except bacteria lacking cell walls such as the mycoplasmas. The structure and function of the bacterial wall is a hallmark of the prokaryotes; it is absent in human cell. • It protects the cell from mechanical disruption and from bursting caused by the internal pressure of the cell. • It also provides a barrier against certain toxic chemical and biologic agents. • Its form is responsible for the shape of the cell. • Site of action of beta lactams (penicillin binding proteins; PBP) • Contains receptor for phages. However, bacterial cell membrane does not contain sterols (except mycoplasmas). 1. Envelope and appendages B. Cell membrane The bacterial cell membrane is therefore the functional equivalent of most of the organelles of the eukaryotic cell and is vital to the growth and maintenance of the cell. 1. Envelope and appendages The cell membrane: • plays a role in the segregation of daughter chromosomes at cell division. • is the site of synthesis of DNA, cell wall polymers. • It contains the entire electron transport system of the cell (and, hence, is functionally analogous to the mitochondria of eukaryotes).

PATHOGENESIS OF BACTERIAL INFECTION Dr. Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 3 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand pathogenesis of infections caused by bacteria Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Define bacterial colonization and infection 2. Recognize the steps of bacterial pathogenesis 3. Relate the virulence mechanisms of bacteria to its pathogenesis 4. Differentiate bacterial exotoxins and endotoxins • Adherence (adhesion, attachment): The process by which bacteria stick to the surfaces of host cells. It is a major initial step in the infection process. • Colonization: the presence of multiplying bacteria on a body surface (like on the skin, mouth, intestines or airway) without causing disease in the person. • Infection: Invasion and Multiplication of an infectious agent within the body to cause disease. • Pathogenicity: The ability of any bacterial species to cause disease in a susceptible human host.

• Infection: Invasion and Multiplication of an infectious agent within the body to cause disease. • Pathogenicity: The ability of any bacterial species to cause disease in a susceptible human host. • Pathogen: A bacterial species able to cause such disease when presented with favorable circumstances (for the organism). • Opportunistic pathogen: An agent capable of causing disease only when the host resistance is impaired ( ie, when the patient is “immunocompromised”). Important definitions Important definitions • Virulence: A term which presumes pathogenicity, but allows expression of degrees from low to extremely high, for example: Low virulence Moderate virulence High virulence Extremely high virulence Streptococcus salivarius oropharyngeal flora, if during a transient bacteremia cause infective endocarditis. Escherichia coli in the colon, but if displacement regularly causes acute infection. Bordetella pertussis , the cause of whooping cough, is not found in the resident flora, highly infectious and causes disease in almost every nonimmune person it contacts.

Yersinia pestis, the cause of plague, is also highly infectious, but in addition leads to death in a few days in over 70% of cases. Attributes of bacterial pathogenicity 1. Entry 2. Adherence 3. Entry • How efficiently bacterial pathogens navigate all these barriers before their initial encounter with their target cell type is in some ways measured by their infecting dose. How many organisms must be given to a host to ensure infection in some proportion of the individuals? • In general, pathogens that have environmental or animal reservoirs can overwhelm innate defenses with large numbers. • Pathogens with no reservoir or amplification mechanism must be transmitted human-to-human and thus require the lowest infecting doses 1. A receptor on the host cell. • The adhesin must be exposed on the bacterial surface either alone or in association with appendages like pili. In gram - negative bacteria, the outer membrane is a major site for adhesins. Most adhesins are proteins, but carbohydrates and teichoic acids may also be involved. • Two of the most common receptors, mannose and fibronectin , are widely present on human epithelial cell surfaces. • Biofilms may also act as an adherence mechanism by binding to catheters, prosthetic devices, or mucosal surfaces. 2. Other bacteria are facultative intracellular pathogens and can grow as free -living cells in the environment as well as within host cells.

Other bacteria are facultative intracellular pathogens and can grow as free -living cells in the environment as well as within host cells. • invasive organisms adhere to host cells by one or more adhesins but use a class of molecules, called invasins, which interact with integrins or other families of cell adhesion molecules. The integrins in turn interact with elements of the cell cytoskeleton stimulating modifications which end in uptake of the bacterial cell. 3. When one of these, serum factor H, is concentrated on the capsular surface, it accelerates the degradation of C3b deposited from the host serum. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 4 Dear students & Transfer Goal Appraise the role of bacterial genetics in medicine Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Recognize all types of bacterial DNA 2. Interpret consequences of genetic change in bacteria 3. Differentiate different types of genetic transfer and exchange 4. Appraise the role of genetic engineering in medicine Types of bacterial DNA Chromosome Plasmid Transposable elements Single circular double stranded supercoiled DNA molecule. Extrachromosomal, double-stranded, circular DNA molecules Pieces of DNA that move readily from one site to another either within or between the DNAs of bacteria, plasmids, and bacteriophages. “jumping genes.” Plasmids carry the genes for the following functions: 1. Antibiotic resistance, (e.g. R plasmids) which is mediated by a variety of enzymes, such as the beta-lactamases. 2. Exotoxins, such as the exfoliative toxin of S. aureus and tetanus toxin of Clostridium tetani.

Pili (fimbriae), which mediate the adherence of bacteria to epithelial cells. Types of bacterial DNA Transmissible plasmid • Transposons are not capable of independent replication; they replicate as part of the DNA in which they are integrated. • Transposons can code for drug- resistant enzymes, toxins, or a variety of metabolic enzymes and can either cause mutations in the gene into which they insert or alter the expression of nearby genes. Types of bacterial DNA Genetic change in bacteria • Mutation • recombination • Transformation • Transduction • Conjugation Genomic Change Exchange of genes • Transposition Within one bacterial cell Between 2 bacterial cells • The spontaneous development of mutations is a major factor in the evolution of bacteria. Mutations occur in nature at a low frequency (one mutation in every million cells for any one gene ), but the large size of microbial populations ensures the presence of many mutants.

Mutations occur in nature at a low frequency (one mutation in every million cells for any one gene ), but the large size of microbial populations ensures the presence of many mutants. • Because bacteria are haploid, the consequences of a mutation, are immediately evident in the mutant cell. Genomic change in bacteria 1. Mutation • Because the generation time of bacteria is short, it does not take many hours for a mutant cell that has arisen by chance to grow to the dominant cell type if the mutation gives it a survival advantage. • Recombination is the process in which nucleic acid molecules from different sources are combined or rearranged to produce a new nucleotide sequence . The source of recombinant DNA may be another part of the same chromosome or from outside the cell from one of the genetic transfer mechanisms described later. Genomic change in bacteria 2. Recombination • There are two types of recombination: a. Homologous recombination occurs between closely related DNA sequences and generally substitutes one sequence for another . The process requires a set of enzymes produced by the rec genes. b.

Homologous recombination occurs between closely related DNA sequences and generally substitutes one sequence for another . The process requires a set of enzymes produced by the rec genes. b. Site-specific recombination occurs between dissimilar DNA sequences and generally produces insertions or deletions or both. This process usually requires specialized recombination enzymes, such as those produced by many transposons and lysogenic bacteriophages. Genomic change in bacteria 2. Recombination • Transposition involves transposable elements that are genetic units capable of mediating their own transfer from one chromosome to another, from one location to another on the same chromosome, or between chromosome and plasmid within the same bacterial cell . This transposition relies on their ability to synthesize their own site -specific recombination enzymes , called transposases. Genetic transfer within bacteria cell Transposition (1) when inserted in a new site they cause insertional mutation. (2) Sometimes they insert into genes and inactivate gene that encodes an essential protein, then the cell dies.

Genetic transfer within bacteria cell Transposition (1) when inserted in a new site they cause insertional mutation. (2) Sometimes they insert into genes and inactivate gene that encodes an essential protein, then the cell dies. (3) The transfer of a transposon to a plasmid and the subsequent transfer of the plasmid to another bacterium by conjugation contributes significantly to the spread of antibiotic resistance. Genetic transfer within bacteria cell Transposition • It involves the release of DNA into the environment by the lysis of some bacterial cells, followed by the direct uptake of that DNA by the recipient cells. The ability to take up DNA from the environment is called competence, and in many species of bacteria. • The fate of the internalized DNA fragment then depends on whether it shares homology (the same or similar base sequences) with a portion of the recipient cell’s DNA. If so, recombination can occur. Heterologous DNA is degraded and causes no heritable change in the recipient cell. Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 1.

• The fate of the internalized DNA fragment then depends on whether it shares homology (the same or similar base sequences) with a portion of the recipient cell’s DNA. If so, recombination can occur. Heterologous DNA is degraded and causes no heritable change in the recipient cell. Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 1. Transformation • Transduction is the transfer of genetic information from donor to recipient cell by viruses of bacteria called bacteriophages. Transduction can be classified as specialized if the phages in question transfer particular genes (usually those adjacent to their integration sites in the genome) or generalized if incorporation of DNA sequences is random because of accidental packaging of host DNA into the phage capsid. The encapsulated DNA, instead of phage DNA, is injected into a new host cell, where it can recombine with the homologous host DNA. Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 2. Transduction Generalized transduction Specialized (Restricted) transduction • The transfer of DNA from the donor to a recipient bacterial cell in a process that requires intimate cell contact . By themselves, bacteria cannot conjugate.

Transduction Generalized transduction Specialized (Restricted) transduction • The transfer of DNA from the donor to a recipient bacterial cell in a process that requires intimate cell contact . By themselves, bacteria cannot conjugate. Only when a bacterial cell contains a self - transmissible plasmid does DNA transfer occur. In most cases, conjugation involves transfer only of plasmid DNA. VIRAL STRUCTURE & CLASSIFICATION Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 7 Dear students & Transfer Goal Recognize viral structure & classification Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Analyze the structural and genomic features of clinically relevant viruses to predict their behavior during infection and transmission. 2. Differentiate enveloped from naked viruses and interpret how their structural differences influence environmental stability, disinfectant susceptibility, and host-cell entry. 3. Apply principles of defective viruses and viral classification to clinical situations involving viral coinfection and viral taxonomy. 4. Evaluate bacteriophage characteristics and propagation patterns to select appropriate phages for potential therapeutic use against bacterial infections.

Apply principles of defective viruses and viral classification to clinical situations involving viral coinfection and viral taxonomy. 4. Evaluate bacteriophage characteristics and propagation patterns to select appropriate phages for potential therapeutic use against bacterial infections. • Viruses are the smallest replicating intracellular microorganisms that are comprised of sets of genes either DNA (DNA viruses) or RNA (RNA viruses) packaged in a capsid (protein shell) or in a capsid and an outer lipid bilayer envelope. • The resulting complete virus particle is called a virion. • Viruses have an obligate requirement for intracellular growth and a heavy dependence on host cell structural and metabolic components. Therefore, viruses are also referred to as obligate intracellular parasites. Viruses do not have a nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, or other cell organelles. Structure of virus • Viruses are approximately 20-400 nm in diameter . • The basic structure of all viruses places the nucleic acid genome ( DNA or RNA) • on the inside of a protein shell called a capsid.

Structure of virus • Viruses are approximately 20-400 nm in diameter . • The basic structure of all viruses places the nucleic acid genome ( DNA or RNA) • on the inside of a protein shell called a capsid. • Some human viruses are further packaged into a lipid membrane, or envelope, which is usually acquired from the plasma or cytoplasmic membrane of the infected cell during release from the cell. Structure of virus • The genomes of enveloped viruses form a protein complex and a structure called a nucleocapsid, • which is often surrounded by a matrix protein that serves as a bridge between the nucleocapsid and the inside of the envelope. • Viruses that are not enveloped have a defined external capsid and are referred to as naked viruses. • Protein or glycoprotein structures called spikes, which often protrude from the surface of virus particles, are involved in the initial contact with receptor on host cells Viral genomes • Viral genomes can be made of either RNA or DNA and also can be either single-stranded or double - stranded.

• Protein or glycoprotein structures called spikes, which often protrude from the surface of virus particles, are involved in the initial contact with receptor on host cells Viral genomes • Viral genomes can be made of either RNA or DNA and also can be either single-stranded or double - stranded. • The RNA viruses can be either positive sense (+) ( same polarity of mRNA) or negative sense (–) (complementary to or antisense of mRNA), double- stranded (one strand + and the second strand –) or ambisense (both + and – polarity on the same strand). • Although the RNA genomes of most viruses are linear, some RNA viruses may also have segmented genomes (several segments or pieces of RNA), with each segment responsible for encoding a protein. The DNA genome of viruses can be both linear and circular genomes. • Most viruses contain a single copy of their genome, except that retroviruses (e.g HIV) carry two identical copies of its genome and are, therefore, diploid. Viral capsids • The capsids or nucleocapsids are virus -encoded specific proteins that protect the genome and confer shapes to viruses.

g HIV) carry two identical copies of its genome and are, therefore, diploid. Viral capsids • The capsids or nucleocapsids are virus -encoded specific proteins that protect the genome and confer shapes to viruses. The capsids of all viruses are composed of many copies of one or, at most, several different kinds of protein subunits . The presence of many identical protein subunits in viral capsids or the existence of many identical spikes in the membrane of enveloped viruses has important implications for adsorption, hemagglutination, and recognition of viruses by neutralizing antibodies. The protein shell forming the capsid or the nucleocapsid assumes one of two basic shapes: helical or icosahedral. Helical Icosahedral Virus envelope • Many human viruses have an outer lipid bilayer membrane that is derived from host plasma membrane. The viral envelope lipid layer membrane contains virus -encoded glycoproteins called “ spikes” or “peplomers” or “viral envelope proteins .

Helical Icosahedral Virus envelope • Many human viruses have an outer lipid bilayer membrane that is derived from host plasma membrane. The viral envelope lipid layer membrane contains virus -encoded glycoproteins called “ spikes” or “peplomers” or “viral envelope proteins .” The envelope spikes bind to the receptor on the host cells, help the virus envelope membrane fuse with the cellular membrane of the host cells, and act as principal antigens against which the host mounts immune response for the recognition of the virus. • Enveloped viruses are more sensitive to detergents, solvents, ethanol, ether, and heat compared with nonenveloped (naked capsid) viruses whose outer coat is capsid protein. • Both envelope glycoproteins, and naked capsid viruses’ spikes become antigens after infection and the host mounts both cell -mediated and humoral immune responses for the elimination of virus -infected cells and cell -free virus, respectively. These antigens also determine the viral serotypes that are based on antigenic variation and are type -specific such as poliovirus serotypes 1, 2, and 3.

• Both envelope glycoproteins, and naked capsid viruses’ spikes become antigens after infection and the host mounts both cell -mediated and humoral immune responses for the elimination of virus -infected cells and cell -free virus, respectively. These antigens also determine the viral serotypes that are based on antigenic variation and are type -specific such as poliovirus serotypes 1, 2, and 3. • The capsid or envelope of viruses functions • (1) to protect the nucleic acid genome from damage during the extracellular passage of the virus from one cell to another, • (2) to aid in the process of entry into the cell, and • (3) in some cases, to package viral enzymes essential for the early steps of the infection process. Defective viruses • Viruses which lack a complete genome so that they cannot completely replicate or cannot form a protein coat. 1. Some are host-dependent defectives, meaning they can replicate only in cell systems which provide the particular genetic function which they lack. 2.

Defective viruses • Viruses which lack a complete genome so that they cannot completely replicate or cannot form a protein coat. 1. Some are host-dependent defectives, meaning they can replicate only in cell systems which provide the particular genetic function which they lack. 2. Others, called Satellite viruses, are able to replicate only when their genetic defect is complemented by a helper virus (is the hepatitis D virus which replicates only in the presence of surface antigen from a co-infecting hepatitis B virus). Reaction to physical & chemical agents Heat and cold Naked viruses tend to be stable, losing little infectivity after several hours at 37 °C. Enveloped viruses are much more heat labile , rapidly at 37 °C. Viral infectivity is generally destroyed by heating at 50 –60°C for 30 minutes, although there are some exceptions (eg, hepatitis B virus) Viruses can be preserved by storage at freezing temperatures, pH Viruses are usually stable between pH values of 5 – 9. Some viruses ( eg, enteroviruses) are resistant to acidic conditions. All viruses are destroyed by alkaline conditions. Radiation Ultraviolet, x-ray inactivate viruses.

Viral infectivity is generally destroyed by heating at 50 –60°C for 30 minutes, although there are some exceptions (eg, hepatitis B virus) Viruses can be preserved by storage at freezing temperatures, pH Viruses are usually stable between pH values of 5 – 9. Some viruses ( eg, enteroviruses) are resistant to acidic conditions. All viruses are destroyed by alkaline conditions. Radiation Ultraviolet, x-ray inactivate viruses. Formaldehyde It destroys viral infectivity by reacting with nucleic acid. Viruses with single-stranded genomes are inactivated much more readily than those with double -stranded genomes. Formaldehyde has minimal adverse effects on the antigenicity of proteins and therefore has been used in the production of inactivated viral vaccines. Chlorine Larger concentrations of chlorine are required to destroy viruses than to kill bacteria, especially in the presence of extraneous proteins. For example, the chlorine treatment of stools adequate to inactivate typhoid bacilli is inadequate to destroy poliomyelitis virus present in feces.

Chlorine Larger concentrations of chlorine are required to destroy viruses than to kill bacteria, especially in the presence of extraneous proteins. For example, the chlorine treatment of stools adequate to inactivate typhoid bacilli is inadequate to destroy poliomyelitis virus present in feces. Quaternary ammonium compounds and organic iodine compounds not effective against viruses Alcohol Alcohols, such as isopropanol and ethanol, are relatively ineffective against certain viruses, especially picornaviruses. Reaction to physical & chemical agents Classification of viruses • The International Committee for Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) considered various properties, including virions, genome, proteins, envelope, replication, and physical and biologic properties. Based on these properties: • virus families are designated with the suffix, -viridae (as in Herpesviridae), • virus subfamilies with suffix virinae (Herpesvirinae), • virus genera with suffix virus (Herpesvirus), and • virus species designated by a virus type (herpes simplex virus 1).

Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 8 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand viral and phage replication cycles Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Why it is difficult to develop antiviral drugs? • Because viruses are obligate intracellular parasites, antiviral agents must be capable of selectively inhibiting viral functions without damaging the host, making the development of such drugs very difficult.

Among the unique viral events are: • attachment, • penetration, • uncoating, • RNA-directed DNA synthesis (reverse transcription) or RNA -directed RNA synthesis (RNA viruses), • assembly and release of the intact virion. • There is a need for antiviral drugs active against viruses for which: • vaccines are not available or not highly effective because of a multiplicity of serotypes (eg, rhinoviruses) • because of constantly changing viral antigens (eg, influenza, HIV).

Clinical benefit depends on the virus, site of infection, host factors, and timing. • Combination therapy is particularly important for viruses with high mutation rates, such as HIV and HCV, because it suppresses replication more effectively and reduces the probability of resistance. PART 1 · STRUCTURE Antigens, serotypes & defective viruses NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 7 Antigens & serotypes Envelope glycoproteins and capsid spikes become antigens after infection The host mounts cell-mediated responses (kill infected cells) and humoral responses (clear cell-free virus) Serotypes: type-specific antigenic variants, e.g. poliovirus types 1, 2 and 3. Defective viruses Lack a complete genome, so they cannot fully replicate or cannot form a protein coat. Host-dependent defectives Replicate only in cells that supply the missing genetic function.

PART 1 · STRUCTURE Reaction to physical & chemical agents NMD3101 · Viral structure, classification & replication · Revision 8 Physical agents Heat Naked viruses are stable; enveloped viruses are heat-labile. Most are inactivated at 50–60 °C for 30 min (exception: hepatitis B virus). Cold Freezing temperatures preserve viruses. pH Stable at pH 5–9; enteroviruses resist acid; all viruses are destroyed by alkali. Radiation Ultraviolet light and X-rays inactivate viruses. Chemical agents Formaldehyde Reacts with nucleic acid (single-stranded genomes are inactivated more readily). Spares protein antigenicity, so it is used for inactivated vaccines.

HEPATITIS C VIRUS Structure of HCV - HCV is the only member of the Hepacivirus genus of the Flaviviridae family. - HCV has a positive-sense RNA genome, and is enveloped. Structure of HCV • The genome encodes 10 proteins , including: • 3 structural [one core protein and two glycoproteins (E1, E2)] as well as • 7 non -structural proteins. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is error prone and generates mutations in the glycoprotein and other genes. This generates antigenic variability. Such variability makes development of a vaccine very difficult. Structure of HCV • There are seven major genotypes (1 -7) of HCV (clades), and between and within each genotype there is considerable genetic and antigenic diversity. Different genotypes predominate in different parts of the world. • Genotype 4a is the most common in Egypt. • HCV Genetic diversity is not correlated with differences in clinical disease, although differences exist in response to antiviral therapy.

text: • Genotype 4a is the most common in Egypt. • HCV Genetic diversity is not correlated with differences in clinical disease, although differences exist in response to antiviral therapy. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV • HCV is transmitted primarily in infected blood and sexually . Intravenous drug abusers and tattoo recipients are at highest risk to HCV infection. Screening procedures have led to a reduction in the levels of transmission by blood transfusion and organ donation. Almost all (>90%) HIV -infected people who are or were intravenous drug users are infected with HCV . Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV • The high incidence of chronic asymptomatic infections promotes the spread of the virus in the population. • The ability of HCV to remain cell associated and prevent host cell death promotes persistent infection but results in liver disease later in life. • The virus’s ability to evade interferon action and change its antigenicity help the virus establish chronic disease. • Cell-mediated immune responses are necessary to resolve the infection but also cause tissue damage. • Antibody to HCV is not protective .

text: • The virus’s ability to evade interferon action and change its antigenicity help the virus establish chronic disease. • Cell-mediated immune responses are necessary to resolve the infection but also cause tissue damage. • Antibody to HCV is not protective . Due to the selective pressure from the host, and the antigenic variations that occur in the E2/E1 proteins, the virus evade the humoral immune response and establish a persistent infection. • HCV antibodies have also been implicated in the formation of immune complexes against the liver and other tissues. During acute infection, the rise in serum transaminases is due to immune -mediated hepatocyte damage. The immune complexes are also deposited in other tissues and cause extrahepatic complications, including vasculitis, arthritis, glomerulonephritis, and others. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV • Chronic HCV infection results in inflammatory response that may lead to progressive fibrosis and hepatocarcinogenesis. • The chronic infection can exhaust CD8 cytotoxic T cells so they cannot resolve the infection. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV Clinical syndromes of HCV • A viremia can be detected within 1 to 3 weeks of infection.

Pathogenesis & Immunity of HCV Clinical syndromes of HCV • A viremia can be detected within 1 to 3 weeks of infection. • The viremia lasts 4 to 6 months in people with an acute infection and longer than 10 years in those with a persistent infection. • The incubation period ranges from 2 weeks to 6 months. • HCV has the highest rate of chronicity (> 75%). • More commonly (>70% of cases), the initial disease is asymptomatic or clinically mild (20–30% have jaundice; 10 –20% have only nonspecific symptoms such as anorexia, malaise, and abdominal pain) but establishes chronic persistent disease . The predominant symptom is chronic fatigue. • Chronic persistent disease often progresses to chronic active hepatitis within 10 to 15 years and to cirrhosis (20% of chronic cases ) and liver failure (20% of cirrhotic cases ) after 20 years. HCV promotes the development of hepatocellular carcinoma after 30 years in up to 5% of chronically infected patients.

This means that for the first eight weeks following exposure to HCV antibody tests may not be able to detect HCV antibodies, and for the first 1-2 weeks following HCV exposure NATs may not be able to detect HCV RNA. Virologic & Serologic Response to HCV • In chronic hepatitis C , serum ALT concentrations may fluctuate over time and may even be intermittently normal. HCV RNA may persist for decades. Diagnosis is confirmed by finding positive anti-HCV and positive HCV - RNA for ≥ 6 months after initial infection.

HEPATITIS B VIRUS Structure of HBV • HBV is the major member of the hepadnaviruses. Other members of this family include woodchuck, ground squirrel, and duck hepatitis viruses. HBV infects the liver and, to a lesser extent, the kidneys and pancreas of only humans and chimpanzees. Structure of HBV • HBV is a small enveloped DNA virus. Specifically, the genome is a small, circular, partly double - stranded DNA . Although a DNA virus, it encodes a reverse transcriptase and replicates through an RNA intermediate. Structure of HBV • The virion, also called the Dane particle, is 42 nm in diameter. The virions are unusually stable for an enveloped virus. They resist treatment with ether, low pH, freezing, and moderate heating . These characteristics assist transmission from one person to another and hamper disinfection.

The virions are unusually stable for an enveloped virus. They resist treatment with ether, low pH, freezing, and moderate heating . These characteristics assist transmission from one person to another and hamper disinfection. The viral genome encodes four overlapping open reading frames (ORFs), C, P , S, and X, from which functional viral proteins are produced: o Hepatitis B Core antigen HBc and its relatives such as E antigen (HBe); HBc: viral capsid protein which is only present inside hepatocytes and detected in liver biopsies and not detected in serum. HBe; It is secreted in a soluble form and detected only in infected patient’s serum. o Pol from P (Polymerase with reverse transcriptase and ribonuclease H activity); o three types of Surface antigens, L-HBs, M-HBs, and S-HBs, (Large, medium and small) from S; o HBV X protein (HBx) from X. Regulatory protein for transcription and is required for initiation of infection. It can be detected only in the cells replicating the virus. Replication of HBV • The attachment of HBV to hepatocytes is mediated by the HBsAg glycoproteins.

Replication of HBV • The attachment of HBV to hepatocytes is mediated by the HBsAg glycoproteins. • On penetration into the cell, the nucleocapsid delivers the genome to the nucleus, where the partial DNA strand of the genome is completed to form a complete double -stranded DNA circle (covalently closed circular DNA; cccDNA) • Transcription of the genome is controlled by cellular transcription elements found in hepatocytes. • Viral genome can be integrated randomly in the host genome . This is not required for viral replication but it is one of the important mechanisms for hepatocyte transformation and HCC development. Replication of HBV Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV • HBV can cause acute or chronic , symptomatic or asymptomatic disease. Which of these occurs seems to be determined by the person’s immune response to the infection. Transmission of HBV • The major source of infectious virus is blood, but HBV can be found in semen, saliva, milk, vaginal secretions, and amniotic fluid.

Which of these occurs seems to be determined by the person’s immune response to the infection. Transmission of HBV • The major source of infectious virus is blood, but HBV can be found in semen, saliva, milk, vaginal secretions, and amniotic fluid. • The most efficient way to acquire HBV is through: • (1) injection of the virus into the bloodstream [Per-cutaneous transmission including intramuscular , intravenous, subcutaneous or intra-dermal injections, tattooing, ear piercing and needle stick. Contamination of skin lesions (fresh cutaneous scratch, abrasion and burns). Infected blood and blood products through transfusion or dialysis. • (2) Common but less efficient routes of infection are sexual contact and birth (Perinatal transmission when mothers are HBsAg positive due to leak of maternal blood to infant’s circulation during birth. Transplacental transmission is rare). • The virus starts to replicate in hepatocytes of the liver within 3 days of its acquisition, with minimal cytopathic effect. • Symptoms may not be observed for 45 days or longer because they are primarily caused by immunopathology.

• The virus starts to replicate in hepatocytes of the liver within 3 days of its acquisition, with minimal cytopathic effect. • Symptoms may not be observed for 45 days or longer because they are primarily caused by immunopathology. • The infectious dose, the route of infection, and the person determine the incubation period. Infection proceeds for a relatively long time without causing liver damage (i.e., elevation of liver enzyme levels) or symptoms. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV • Copies of the HBV genome integrate into the hepatocyte DNA and can remain latent. HBsAg particles continue to be released into the blood even after virion release has ended and until the infection is resolved. • An individual is infectious when both the HBsAg and the HBeAg components of the virion can be detected in the blood. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV • Cell-mediated immunity and inflammation are responsible for causing the symptoms and effecting resolution of the HBV infection by eliminating the infected hepatocyte.

Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV • Cell-mediated immunity and inflammation are responsible for causing the symptoms and effecting resolution of the HBV infection by eliminating the infected hepatocyte. • An insufficient T-cell response to the infection generally results in the occurrence of mild symptoms, an inability to resolve the infection, and development of chronic hepatitis. • Chronic infection also exhausts CD8 T cells, preventing them from killing infected cells. Infants and young children have an immature cell - mediated immune response and are less able to resolve the infection, but they suffer less tissue damage and milder symptoms. • As many as 90% of infants infected perinatally become chronic carriers. Viral replication persists in these people for long periods. Pathogenesis & Immunity of HBV Immune Response to HBV inability to resolve the infection, and development of chronic hepatitis effecting resolution of the HBV infection by eliminating the infected hepatocyte.

Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 12 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand antifungal agents and their resistance mechanisms Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Differentiate the mechanisms of action of major antifungal drug classes based on their fungal cellular targets. 2. Interpret the clinical spectrum and pharmacologic properties of antifungal agents to guide treatment of common and life-threatening fungal infections. 3. Select an appropriate antifungal agent for a patient according to the fungal pathogen, site/severity of infection, and important drug toxicities. 4. Analyze antifungal resistance mechanisms by relating changes in drug targets, drug uptake, efflux, or biosynthetic pathways to therapeutic failure. • Compared with antibacterial agents, relatively few antifungals are available for treatment of fungal infections.

Analyze antifungal resistance mechanisms by relating changes in drug targets, drug uptake, efflux, or biosynthetic pathways to therapeutic failure. • Compared with antibacterial agents, relatively few antifungals are available for treatment of fungal infections. Many substances with antifungal activity have proved to be unstable, to be toxic to humans , or to have undesirable pharmacologic characteristics, such as poor diffusion into tissues. Newer antifungal agents target fungal -specific cellular features and demonstrate lower toxicity than older drug classes. Mechanism of action of antifungals I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Action: The polyenes nystatin and amphotericin B are lipophilic and bind to ergosterol , the dominant sterol in the cytoplasmic membrane of fungal cells. After binding, they form annular channels, which penetrate the membrane and lead to leakage of essential small molecules from the cytoplasm and cell death. 1. Polyenes I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Spectrum of activity: Almost all fungi are susceptible to amphotericin B , and the development of resistance is rare.

Use of amphotericin B is limited to progressive, life-threatening fungal infections. • Amphotericin B is insoluble in water and must be administered intravenously as a colloidal suspension • Side effects: The major limitation to amphotericin B therapy is the toxicity created by its affinity for mammalian as well as fungal membranes. Intravenous Infusion is commonly followed by chills, fever, headache, and dyspnea. The most serious toxic effect is renal dysfunction . The even greater toxicity of nystatin limits its use to topical preparations 1. Polyenes I. Antifungals acting on cell membrane • Action: Their activity is based on inhibition of the enzyme “lanosterol 14-α-demethylase” responsible for conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol, the major component of the fungal cell membrane. This leads to ergosterol depletion and lanosterol accumulation, forming defective membranes. 2. Azoles Azoles are generally fungistatic against many fungi rather than uniformly fungicidal. I. Mold-active azoles (itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, and isavuconazole) have extended activity against molds such as Aspergillus species . II. Antifungals acting on nucleic acid synthesis • Action: 5-Flucytosine (5FC) is an analog of cytosine. It is a potent inhibitor of RNA transcription and DNA synthesis. Flucytosine II. Antifungals acting on nucleic acid synthesis • Spectrum of activity: Flucytosine is well absorbed after oral administration. It is active against most clinically important yeasts, including Candida albicans and Cryptococcus neoformans, but it has little activity against molds. • Side effects: The frequent development of mutational resistance during therapy limits its application to mild yeast infections or its use in combination with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis . The primary toxic effect of flucytosine is a reversible bone marrow suppression that can lead to neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Flucytosine III.

Echinocandin administration, therefore, causes morphologic distortions and osmotic instability in yeasts and molds, similar to the effect of β-lactams on bacteria. Echinocandins III. Although highly active against many Candida species, the echinocandins tend to be used as second -line agents for invasive aspergillosis. Cryptococcus neoformans whose cell wall glucans have a slightly different structure, are more tolerant of echinocandins. • Newer echinocandins, micafungin and anidulafungin, have the same mode of action and a similar spectrum of antifungal activity. • Side effects: Since there are no similar glucans in humans, echinocandin toxicity is minimal. Echinocandins IV . Other antifungals Griseofulvin • Action: acts on the microtubules and associated proteins that make up the mitotic spindle. It interferes with cell division. • Spectrum of activity : after oral administration, it is absorbed from GIT and concentrates in the keratinized layers of the skin. It is active only against the agents of superficial mycoses. • Side effects : Clinical response is slow. Prolonged therapy may be required. To Sum Up Antifungal resistance • Many of the same resistance mechanisms observed in bacteria are also found in fungi. • Fungi tend to primarily inactivate drug activity using efflux pumps and by altering their biosynthetic pathways.

To Sum Up Antifungal resistance • Many of the same resistance mechanisms observed in bacteria are also found in fungi. • Fungi tend to primarily inactivate drug activity using efflux pumps and by altering their biosynthetic pathways. • In contrast to bacteria, fungi do not make hydrolytic enzymes to inactivate antibiotics to the same extent as bacteria.

PRINCIPLES OF VACCINES Dr . Marwa A. Meheissen Professor of Medical Microbiology & Immunology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Email: marwa.meheissen@alexmed.edu.eg NMD3101 Principles of infection Lecture 13 Dear students & Transfer Goal Understand the principle and types of vaccines Students’ learning outcomes • At the end of this session, the student will be able to: 1. Define vaccine and Recognize the principle of vaccination 2. Classify different types of vaccines 3. Differentiate between inactivated and live attenuated vaccines 4. Identify the advantages and disadvantages of different types of vaccines 5. Relate different types of vaccines to the generated immune response What is vaccine? • The word “vaccine” originates from the Latin Variolae vaccinae (cowpox), which Edward Jenner demonstrated in 1798 could prevent smallpox in humans. Today the term ‘vaccine’ applies to all biological preparations, produced from living organisms, that enhance immunity against disease and either prevent (prophylactic vaccines) or, in some cases, treat disease (therapeutic vaccines). • Vaccines are administered in liquid form, either by injection, by oral, or by intranasal routes.

Today the term ‘vaccine’ applies to all biological preparations, produced from living organisms, that enhance immunity against disease and either prevent (prophylactic vaccines) or, in some cases, treat disease (therapeutic vaccines). • Vaccines are administered in liquid form, either by injection, by oral, or by intranasal routes. Principle of vaccination • Vaccines artificially stimulate immunity through exposure to an antigenic substance. • An effective vaccine does not protect against disease until it is administered in the proper dosage to susceptible individuals. • Failure to reach all sectors of the population with complete courses of immunization is reflected in the continued occurrence of outbreaks in populations who refuse immunization. • Active immunization → vaccine → slower onset → memory → long-term protection • Passive immunization → antibody → immediate protection → temporary → no memory • Herd immunity refers to the fact that the risk of infection among susceptible individuals in a population is reduced by the presence of adequate numbers of immune individuals.

• Active immunization → vaccine → slower onset → memory → long-term protection • Passive immunization → antibody → immediate protection → temporary → no memory • Herd immunity refers to the fact that the risk of infection among susceptible individuals in a population is reduced by the presence of adequate numbers of immune individuals. However, the threshold of immunity needed for this indirect protective effect depends on many factors, including the transmissibility of the infectious agent, the nature of the vaccine- induced immunity, and the distribution of the immune individuals. Principle of vaccination Herd immunity Vaccines are composed of either the entire disease-causing microorganism or some of its components. • From living organisms that have been weakened, usually from cultivation under sub -optimal conditions (also called attenuation), or from genetic modification, which has the effect of reducing their ability to cause disease; • From whole organisms that have been inactivated by chemical, thermal or other means; Vaccines are composed of either the entire disease-causing microorganism or some of its components.

Types of bacterial DNA Transmissible plasmid •Transposonsare not capable of independent replication; they replicate as part of the DNA in which they are integrated. •Transposons can code for drug-resistant enzymes,toxins, or a variety of metabolic enzymes and can either cause mutations in the gene into which they insert or alter the expression of nearby genes. Types of bacterial DNA Genetic change in bacteria • Mutation • recombination • Transformation • Transduction • Conjugation Genomic Change Exchange of genes • Transposition Within one bacterial cell Between 2 bacterial cells •The spontaneous development of mutations is a major factor in the evolution of bacteria. Mutations occur in nature at a low frequency(one mutation in every million cells for any one gene), but the large size of microbial populations ensures the presence of many mutants.

Mutations occur in nature at a low frequency(one mutation in every million cells for any one gene), but the large size of microbial populations ensures the presence of many mutants. •Because bacteria are haploid, the consequences of a mutation, are immediately evident in the mutant cell. Genomic change in bacteria 1. Mutation •Because the generation time of bacteria is short, it does not take many hours for a mutant cell that has arisen by chance to grow to the dominant cell type if the mutation gives it a survival advantage. •Recombination is the process in which nucleic acid molecules from different sources are combined or rearrangedto produce a new nucleotide sequence. The source of recombinant DNA may be another part of the same chromosome or from outside the cell from one of the genetic transfer mechanisms described later . Genomic change in bacteria 2. Recombination •There are two types of recombination: a.Homologous recombinationoccurs between closely related DNA sequences and generally substitutes one sequence for another . The process requires a set of enzymes produced by the recgenes. b.

Homologous recombinationoccurs between closely related DNA sequences and generally substitutes one sequence for another . The process requires a set of enzymes produced by the recgenes. b.Site-specificrecombinationoccurs between dissimilar DNA sequences and generally produces insertions or deletions or both. This process usually requires specialized recombination enzymes, such as those produced by many transposons and lysogenic bacteriophages. Genomic change in bacteria 2. Recombination •Transposition involves transposable elements that are genetic units capable of mediating their own transfer from one chromosome to another, from one location to another on the same chromosome, or between chromosome and plasmid within the same bacterial cell . This transposition relies on their ability to synthesize their own site-specific recombination enzymes, called transposases. Genetic transfer within bacteria cell Transposition (1) when inserted in a new site they cause insertional mutation. (2) Sometimes they insert into genes and inactivate gene that encodes an essential protein, then the cell dies.

(2) Sometimes they insert into genes and inactivate gene that encodes an essential protein, then the cell dies. (3) The transfer of a transposon to a plasmid and the subsequent transfer of the plasmid to another bacterium by conjugation contributes significantly to the spread of antibiotic resistance. Genetic transfer within bacteria cell Transposition •It involves the release of DNA into the environment by the lysis of some bacterial cells, followed by the direct uptake of that DNA by the recipient cells. The ability to take up DNA from the environment is called competence, and in many species of bacteria. •The fate of the internalized DNA fragment then depends on whether it shares homology (the same or similar base sequences) with a portion of the recipient cell’s DNA. If so, recombinationcan occur . Heterologous DNA is degradedand causes no heritable change in the recipient cell. Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 1. Transformation •Transduction is the transfer of genetic information from donor to recipient cell by viruses of bacteria called bacteriophages.

Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 1. Transformation •Transduction is the transfer of genetic information from donor to recipient cell by viruses of bacteria called bacteriophages. Transduction can be classified as specializedif the phages in question transfer particular genes (usually those adjacent to their integration sites in the genome) or generalizedif incorporation of DNA sequences is random because of accidental packaging of host DNA into the phage capsid. The encapsulated DNA, instead of phage DNA, is injected into a new host cell, where it can recombine with the homologous host DNA. Genetic transfer between bacterial cells 2. Transduction Generalized transduction Specialized (Restricted) transduction •The transfer of DNA from the donor to a recipient bacterial cell in a process that requires intimate cell contact. By themselves, bacteria cannot conjugate. Only when a bacterial cell contains a self- transmissible plasmid does DNA transfer occur . In most cases, conjugation involves transfer only of plasmid DNA. Many substances with antifungal activity have proved to be unstable, to be toxic to humans, or to have undesirable pharmacologic characteristics, such as poor diffusion into tissues. Newer antifungal agents target fungal-specific cellular features and demonstrate lower toxicity than older drug classes. Mechanism of action of antifungals I.

Many substances with antifungal activity have proved to be unstable, to be toxic to humans, or to have undesirable pharmacologic characteristics, such as poor diffusion into tissues. Newer antifungal agents target fungal-specific cellular features and demonstrate lower toxicity than older drug classes. Mechanism of action of antifungals I. Today the term ‘vaccine’ applies to all biological preparations, produced from living organisms, that enhance immunity against disease and either prevent (prophylactic vaccines) or, in some cases, treat disease (therapeutic vaccines). •Vaccines are administered in liquid form, either by injection, by oral, or by intranasal routes.

Principle of vaccination •Vaccines artificially stimulate immunity through exposure to an antigenic substance. •An effective vaccine does not protect against disease until it is administered in the proper dosage to susceptible individuals. •Failure to reach all sectors of the population with complete courses of immunization is reflected in the continued occurrence of outbreaks in populations who refuse immunization. •Herd immunity refers to the fact that the risk of infection among susceptible individuals in a population is reduced by the presence of adequate numbers of immune individuals. Definition Myiasis is a zoonosis derived from the Greek word (mya, or fly) . Myiasis is the infestation of live vertebrates (humans and/or animals) with larvae of medium -sized and large dipterous flies. These larvae (Maggots) can feed on the host's living or dead tissue, liquid body substance, or ingested food. Risk factors Myiasis in humans is distributed world wide but more common in tropics and sub-tropical regions. Low socioeconomic state and poor hygienic measures are main risk factors. Myiasis is considered an important Traveler-associated skin disease. Nosocomial infestations are not uncommon. Causative agent Larvae of flies (Maggots) are the causative agents of myiasis.

Furuncular myiasis The main clinical presentation in this form is a boil -like lesion (furuncle) that occurs due to penetration of healthy skin with the larvae of bot flies (screw worms) mainly Dermatobia hominis and Cordylobia anthropophaga. Migratory (Creeping) myiasis This type of myiasis occurs when the maggots accidentally infest unnatural host. Figure 4 3. Wound myiasis This form of myiasis occurs when flies oviposit or larviposit on open wounds especially those necrotic and pus-filled. Wound myiasis is common in neglected individuals. Elderly debilitated patients, psychiatric illness, wars and human natural disasters are the common risk factors for wound myiasis. The condition can be complicated by destruction and deep invasion in tissues together with superadded bacterial infection. The most common flies causing wound myiasis are Sarcophaga, Lucilia and Calliphora flies. Cavitary myiasis This term applies to infestation of body cavities and internal organs with maggots. 1.

Intestinal myiasis Intestinal infestation with maggots occurs accidentally when ingesting food or drinks contaminated with eggs or larvae of flies. The condition is facilitated by low gastric acidity. The passage of larvae in stool samples is diagnostic. Larvae can pass to t he intestinal passages up from anal orifice while sleeping outdoors (naked children) or by the use of open latrines. The condition can be associated with nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. Pruritus ani and rectal bleeding are not uncommon. Common flies causing intestinal myiasis are Musca domestica and Fannia spp. 2. Urogenital myiasis This is a form of accidental myiasis where the flies deposit their eggs or larvae on the external urinary or genital orifices. Maggots can cause lesions in the external genitalia or ascends up and cause internal urogenital myiasis. The condition is more common in females and children.

Urogenital myiasis This is a form of accidental myiasis where the flies deposit their eggs or larvae on the external urinary or genital orifices. Maggots can cause lesions in the external genitalia or ascends up and cause internal urogenital myiasis. The condition is more common in females and children. The main risk factors are low hygienic measures, the use of open latrines and sleeping outdoors, especially children lacking underwear. The main clinical presentations include dysuria, haematuria, pruritus and ureteric obstruction and all are relieved by extrusion of maggots in urine. Page 4 of 6 3. Ophthalmomyiasis This condition is considered when there is a foreign body sensation in the eye with an abrupt pain. The conjunctiva is mostly affected. Redness, excessive lacrimation and superadded infection are the main clinical presentation. Oestrus spp. (sheep flies) are the main agents responsible and the condition can be more common in shepherds, children and neglected debilitated individuals. Ecological classification: Specific/Obligatory myiasis The fly is obligatory dependent on the host to complete its life cycle and the larvae are usually provided with strong and sharp mouth parts to screw into healthy host tissues. The larvae feed on the host till the time of pupation and then drop out to complete its life cycle. Dermatobia hominis and Cordylobia anthropophaga are the main examples causing furuncular myiasis in humans. Hypoderma and Gastrophilus flies cause specific creeping myiasis in man. Risk factors: Moving with bare feet or sitting naked on sandy soil soaked with urine. The flies are attracted and deposit their eggs on these areas and hence the eggs hatch and larvae are attracted to the warmth of the skin. Larvae penetrate healthy skin with their sharp mouth parts and cause furuncular lesion.

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم صباح الخير يا شباب ان شاء الله النهارده هنتكلم في المحاضره دي عن البيزك اوف بكتيريا وازاي بنعمل لها كلاسيكيشن والبكتيريا دي بالجروب ازاي علشان يبقى عندنا بيزك انفورميشن تفيدنا بعد كده ان شاء الله في المحاضرات الجايه اللي هنتكلم فيها شويه بقى عن الانفاكشنز بتحصل ازاي وبنعالج الحاجات ازاي فلازم نبقى عارفين بس بيزك شويه بيزك عن البكتيري ا طيب هي البكتيريا من ضمن الميكروب اورجنز احنا عرفنا في المحاضره يمكن اللي فاتت اللي هي كانت انتروداكشن ان هي تصنف من البروكاريوتس خليه بدائيه بتاعها بيتقاس بالمايكروز يعني فارس ومع ذلك ومع ذلك بتتشاف العادي انا لسه مش محتاجه اكتر زي مثلا الفيروس بس علشان صغرها وعلشان هي غري بنقول عليها ما لهاش لون بنضطر نصبوها فالصبغه المشهوره قوي في البكتيريا حاجه اسمها جرام ستريم دي اسم الساين اللي قال حنسبق البكتيريا بالجرام قسمت البكتيريا الى توميجر جروبس ودي اللي هنلاقيها في الكلاسيكيشن في اخر المحاضره يا اما جريند يا اما جرام لونها ابيض طيب هيفيدنا في ايه الكلام ده ان احنا بعد كده هيطلع لي بتاع الميكروبيولوجي بتاع المعمل لما الفيش يبقى عنده يقول لي والله دي شكلها جرام وهطلع لك بكره بكره او دي شكلها لازم ابقى عارف يعني ايه طيب هنقول بالتفاصيل بقى كمان شويه اشكال بقى البكتيريا غير السايز بتاعها اللي هي نص نيكرون او ممكن توصل لتان ميكروز

بكتيريا قوي اللي بتقبل حجمها كبير كده لكن معظمهم نص واحد وهكذا اشكالها ايه معظم البكتيريا في الدنيا يا اما يعني اللي بيقولوا عليها خليه زي الكوره يا اما بس خليه زي العصايه معظمهم كده او ممكن نلاقي شويه اكسبشنز او بقى مورفولوجي زي الكمشيت زي السبايل شيب زي الفيلمنتس حاجات غريره زي بلايك ممكن تاخذ كذا شكل بس الاساس هي دايره او كوره يا اما عصاري معظم البكتيريا زي ما قلنا جرام او مش معظم يعني هنقول لك كلاسيكيه دي كمان شويه بس هي اساس الكلاسيكيشن يجران باز في جرام ونقدر نقول ان كل البكتيريا جرام يا جرام ما بتاخدش صبغه الجرام هنقولها في اخر المحاضره ان شاء الله ويا اما تبقى عصويه زي اللي على الشمال كده تحت عصايه لونها فايلوت يا اما الكوره او كوكاي لونها فوق على الشمال او على اليمين السلايد فوق عندنا الكوكاي لونه احمر او بس اللاي لونها احمر بتاعها حاجه خارجيه اللي بيسموها اللي حوالين البكتيريا او الانفان الحاجات الاكستراز اللي مع الانفلوك والانتير كور او الحاجه اللي جوه البكتيريا او الاستراكتير اللي جوه بتاعتها تعتمد ميلي او دهل الاساسي اللي في البكتيريا اللي مش موجود عندنا وده اللي بيعتمد على البورت في الميكروب لما اجي اعالج طب ما انا عندي هنقوله دلوقتي مش موجود في طب ما انا اعالج البكتيريا ان انا ادي انتباهه بيكسر ده فمش هياثر على طيب القلب ده بيتكون من ايه وده بقى اللي بقول لكم عليه

مش موجود في الايه ما في الخليه نحطوها في ما عندهاش حاجه اسمها سلوى السلول ده عباره عن ايه ماده غالبا هنشوف الفرق بيننا بين جرام دلوقتي البكتيريا الجرام عندهم سلول بتعمل بروتكشن بارير لاي طقس بتدي الشيب للبكتيريا عليها هو مش قاعد عشان يمسك الفانيليا بس هو له نور س بتاعه السلوول وكمان بالمره طب انا هستخدمك ان البنسلين يمسك في ريسبتور اللي عليك علشان انا انت براتك اشتغل عليك وكمان عندها ريسبتور بكتيريا هنقول البكتيري فاج كمان محاضرتين كده طيب بتاعها هو متشابه فيما عدا ان كان حاجه اسمها كبيره قوي في الجرام تستبدل يعني تعتبر 80% من الثقل هي كلها نيجي على الجرام لكن حوالي خمسه وبقيتها حاجه اسمها اوترمن تستبدل بحاجه اسمها اوتر طيب ارسال وول اتفقنا السالب ما بين هنتكلم عليه كمان شويه انا بتكلم على الحته اللي فوق دي اللي هي ميليكات هنقول بتاعه كمان شويه هو عباره عن السلوي بتاع جرام من جلوكوز او سكريات معها يتخللها حاجه اسمها تيكويك اسيد نوع من انواع برضو السكريات او لايك وتيكويك اسيد اللي هي الميجر بتاعه جرام يبقى بتاعه الجرام البكتيريا ما هي الا شويه سكريات بس ابقى فاهم ان هتفيدني في ايه دي هتفيدني برضو في علاج البكتيريا لان معظم الانتيبيوتك اللي بتشتغل على محتاجه تشتغل على بتوقفه يبقى هتشتغل على جرام اكتر ما تشتغل على الفرام لان زي ما قلنا في السلايد اللي فاتت بكتير لكن اقل شويه طيب زي

ما قلنا الجرام ناجت البكتيريا هي ايه السالبول بتاعها مكون من ايه رفيعه شويه تم استبدالها بحاجه اسمها اوتر ميمبرين عباره عن توليرس اينر زي السلم بين العادي بتاعه بتاعي بتاع اللي تحت ده الحته اللي جوه دي ما فيهاش مشكله وشبه لليومنت الحته اللي بره الابشر بتاع الاوتر من دي بقى اللي هو عباره عن ايه حاجه ماده اسمها او اسمه مكون من 3 مكون من ليبيد ايه وكور بوليس اللي هو الحته النهائيه او السيرفيست ستربشر بتاع من شكل الحاجه دي عندي حاجتين مهمين في اللايكوبوليس البكتيريا زي ما قلنا في الجرام يعتبر الانتجن بتاع الجرام طازجتيريا في الجرام هو الانتجن بتاع الجرام تمام امال ايه يعتبر الطقس بتاع الغرام حاجه بنسميها الكلينكلين عنده مشكله كبيره ان مش بس البكتيريا دخلت عمليه الانفاكشن ده البكتيريا لما بتتكسر ويطلع تتكسر يعني ايه ابتدت بقى البكتيل الكبيره تموت والبكتيريا الصغيره تعمل وتطلع في البكتيريا الاولد اللي بتموت دي بتتكسر وتموت السالبول بتاعها في ماده اسمها اللي هو عنده يعني ايه نوع من انواع التاكسي هناخده في المحاضره اللي جايه ان شاء الله هنشوف بيعمل ايه وانبشن ازاي ممكن يدخل في طقس عنده تقسيميه او سابتك شهر اللي هي بنسميها التسمم الدم البسيط الموجود في الغرام هنلاقيه في السلايد اللي فاتت له علاقه بالبورينز وليه علاقه بالايه زي البروتين كده بسيطه بتدخل بتطلع عارفه برضو ان في ستركشر في

البتاع الجرام ناجت البكتيري اسمه كده في تاني في الجرام يختلف عن الجرام اللي هو اسمه عباره عن ايه عباره بس عن ان هو موجود بين السلوول والسايتوب ده بيبقى فيه البكتيريا اللي ناويه تكسر هتبقى وغيره لما هنعرف يعني ايه بيتميزز كمان شويه في السبيس ده وتحوشوا لغايه لما البكتيريا تتعرض للانتيباتك فايه تعرض البكتيريا للانزاين الانتباه ده فبالتالي يحصل ديسكريبشن للبكتيريا للانتي فهتبقى ريزيست وجود الانتباه طيب يبقى من الكلام اللي احنا قلناه موجود في جرام موجود بس فيريسيك في الجرامك فقط اللي هو موجود في جرام فقط وليس موجود في الجرام وزي ما قلنا هنقوله كمان شويه زي السلم بريم بتاع الهيوم موجود هنا وهنا هنشوف بقى يعني ايه ان انا لما اتعرض اسمه يقدر يكسر البكتيريا السل بتاع الجرام هنشوفه كمان شويه ايه اللي بيحصل ده ما بيشتغلش على الجرام ده هستفيد منه بعد كده في حاجات له علاقه بالعلاج بالعلاج بتاع البكتيريا او لما اكسرها فاعرف انه بيشتغل بس على جرام فاز البكتيريا مش هيشتغل جرام لانه بيكسر وبما ان اميجر ستراكتور يبقى هياثر اكثر من الجرام نفس القصه بما اني كابتنن او انتباه هشتغل على اللير اللي اسمها هناخد في محاضره الانتباهوتكس يبقى هاقصر اكتر الجرام باز على جرام ناجت البكتيريا وعرفنا طبعا والتانيه احمر طيب نتكلم شويه عشان نفهم شويه القصه دي هي عباره عن لير من السكريات اتفقنا حاجه اسمها متركبه في

حاجه اسمها انا عباره عن شيتس زي الليرز كده فوق بعضها متركبه مع بعض بتضرب لينك ببعضها بتنتجلاسين كراس لينك ما يهمناش في الاخر الشيت ده زي ما احنا شايفين ادي الاخضر مثلا انا ماسك في ان اسيتايتلوكوزامين نازل من ان ستايل ميراميك اسيد الانينو مش عارفه ايه وايه ولايصين وقلمين دي ماسكه في اختها اللي جنبها بتنتجلاسين يعني يعتبر شويه امايمو اسيد ماسكه في الايه في اللير الاحمر والاخضر بتاعه الايه الجلوكوز فعشان كده قلنا او الجلايك او الكربوهيدرات عشان كده قلنا ان هي ليرميلي اوفرز طيب عرفنا ان هي شبكه كده معقده وماسكه في بعضها ده اللي بيخلي ان السلوي بتاعك اوفاريت ترامب طيب زي ما قلنا بتقدر نقصر على ده موجود في ايه موجود فين مثلا الدموع بتاعتنا فيها فعشان كده دايما البكتيريا الموجوده على وشي انا لما بنزل الدموع اللي من وشي دي ما يبقاش في اي لان انا السكين بتاعي او موجود الميه اللي نازله من عيني دي مليانه دي بتكسر السلول بتاع اللي هي معظم البكتيريا الموجوده على معظمها جرام فاحمي نفسي ويبقى صورته اكروتكشن فلما اجي اشوف ديزاين ده بيا ثر عليه بيعمل بيبلوك الفورميشن ده يجي على الكراس لينك اللي بين اللي هي اللي قلنا بتعمل بين الشيتس بتاعه الجلوكوز ليرز او بتاعه الكربوهيدليه ليرز يكسرها فمن الاخر بيكسر بس لقوا بقى ان انا لو عرضت البكتيريا ليه خلاص كسرها بس لو عرضت البكتيريا نفسها دي ليه انت اسمه ده

بيعمل نفس تقريبا الفانكشن او الاكشن بتاعه الليزوزين بيكسل لقوا ان هو البكتيريا لما تتعرض بس تبقى في انفايرومنت بيقولوا عليه ايزوتونيك يعني جوه وبره من حيث الاملاح ايكوال هتلاقي ان هو البكتيريا دي بتتحول ان السلوول فقط هو اللي اتكسر وما اقدرش اعمل حاجه بعد كده في البكتيريا دي ان هي تبقى زي ما هنعرف مع الفانيل في ان هو بيكسر البكتيري كلها ويحصل لها فتتحول البكتيريا دي من حاجه اسمها فول فيجيتيت البكتيريا لحاجه اسمها يعني من الاخر عشان ما تتلخبطش في الحته دي ان البكتيريا المفترض لما تتعرض للتانيث تتكسر وتموت لا في انواع من البكتيريا اللي بتبقى في انفايرومنت معين وده بيحصل اثناء العلاج انا بقول الحته دي عشان ساعات تبتدي كورس علاج بفني تلاقيه بيستجيب في الاول تيجي بعد فتره تلاقي ايه حصل او ما نقدرش نقول عليها نقدر نقول ان هي ريلاكس او نقدر نقول ان هي هو ما خفش اساسا لان ابتدا شويه في اول كم ساعه او اول كم يوم يبتدي وبعد كده كل الخلايا البكتيريا تحولت من فيجيتيت البكتيريا تقدر تستجيب لنوع ستيتش معين من البكتيريا يبقى اسمه بروتوكلاس والبروتوبلاس ده عباره عن ايه البكتيريا فقدت السالبول بس هي لسه عايشه انا مش عايزه كده انا مش عايزه لما اعرض للفان يسلم ان انا البكتيريا لسه عايشه هي لسه ما زالت عايشه ولسه ما زالت بتعملي انفكشن انا مش عايز كده انا عايز لما اتعرض للبكتيريا تموت انا اسفه

الانتيبيوتك ده يكسر البكتيريا وخلاص لا انا لما بتعرض لها في الظروف معينه بتتحول الى البروتوبلاست هو البكتيريا كلها على بعضها فيما عدا السلبول بتاعها طيب خلينا يعني المعلومه دي في دماغنا لغايه لما ناخدها نستفيد بها في حته تانيه طيب يبقى ده الاكشن ان هو موجود في بتاع الغرام فهو بيشتغل على هيقدر يكسرها فبالتالي انا كسرت البكتيريا نيجي نشوف الجرام مش هيشتغل عليها لان السلم والاكتوريته اكتر من بين وليس فهو عشان يدخل ويلاقي مكان مش عارف يدخل فعشان كده اللايز مش بيشتغل على الجرام ده كتير طيب نيجي بقى على اساس بنتكلم عليه بتفاصيل شويه ما هو الا سكريات برضو حاجه اسمها سكريات وعرفنا ان هو الميجر بتاع مش مطلوب مننا نعرف اكتر من كده طيب اللايك بورد الاكسترن بتاع الاوتور من بتاع الجرام اتفقنا ان هو عباره عن 3 سترابتورز في بعض اللي هو الاساسي بتاع البكتيريا اليمين سيستم بعد كده يتعرف على ان البكتيريا دخلت من الاو انتجن ده سكرايت هنعرف كمان يعني يمكن في حته تانيه كمان ان البكتيريا الوحيده اللي ما عندهاش اللي عندها ستيرل في السلم بريم بتاعها حاجه اسمها مايكوبلازم البكتيريا يسال من بريم بقى لازم نبقى عارفين ان هو بيتيك كثير لان احنا عارفين احنا يمكن قلنا الكلام ده في المحاضره اللي فاتت البكتيريا دي ما هي الا تحتيها سلمى بريم السلم برين جوه في سايتوبلاز في جينوم او الكروموسوم وشويه ديان ايه وشويه

بس خلصنا كده الاستربش وشويه حاجات هنقولها كمان شويه فبالتالي انا اللي عندي مايتوكندريا طب انا هتصرف ازاي كبكتيريا السمن بريم بالتيك بقى هنلاقي ان بتلعب رال انسان ديفيجن بتاع البكتيريا لبروتين تعدي الحاجات الكويسه وتطلع الحاجات وما تدخلش الحاجات الايه البروتين لها علاقه بتق سيمز وانزاينز البكتيريا هتطلعها بعد كده عشان تعمل الانفاكشن هنلاقي ان السمن برين السلوول اللي اتكلمنا عليه من شويه وقلنا هو مفيش حاجه تانيه عندها السالون احنا من اول المحاضره بنتكلم بس على اوكي ده مع انه مهم بس ما يعملش تقريبا غير بروتكشن وعليه شويه ريسبتور لكن السلمرين كل الفانكز بتاعه البكتيريا تقع في لسان بيطلق عليها اسم علميا لو هي يعني شويه جلي كده ما لوش تراكتور محدد حوالين البكتيريا بقول عليها سلايم لير لو ليها واضح وصريح بقول عليها ايه كبسول تمام لو طيب شغلته الاساسيه انت فجوستك وهنتكلم عليها بالتفاصيل الممله بيعمل ايه لان دي مهمه في بتاعه البكتيريا لما تدخل في محاضره الباس طيب ايه تاني في الخارجي للبكتيريا موجود حاجه اسمها فلاجيلاي دي عباره عن اهداف هيرلاكشن هدفها ايه الزق على سطح الخليه اللي هعمل لها انفكشن البكتيريا لما بتيجي تعمل انفكشن هنشوف في المحاضره بتاعه البكتيريا الان هي محتاجه نمبر وان تلزق على سطح الخليه فهتلزق بايه طيب في نوع تاني من البيلاي او الاهداف اسمه هنتكلم عليها بالتفاصيل في محاضره

الجيناتكس بتاعه البكتيريا هل البكتيريا جيناتكس مهمه مهمه جدا وبتستخدم في الموليك للبيولوجي وهنعرفها بالتفصيل في المحاضره في طيب يعني البكتيريا هل فيه هم ليه سموها سكس علشان يعني بيقولوا ان هي اكنها والتانيه اكنها يعني مجازن تمام في بروسس اسمه كونجبيشن طيب امال ايه الفلاجيل اللي بيسموه بالعربي الصوت او الصوت بتاع البكتيريا اللي هو ايه اللي هو عباره عن الحاجه اللي بتتحرك اكنه الديري او الحاجه اللي بتتحرك بها البكتيريا الموجوده على السلايد اهو الديل ده عباره عن ايه موتيليتي فقط احنا قلنا احنا فين احنا في الكور بتاع البكتيريا سيتوبلازم جواه شويه ريبوز جوه نيوكليوس ما اقدرش اقول عليها الكلمه اللي انا قلتها من شويه مش صح اسمها لان هي لا ترقى الى النيوكليوس هي عباره عن انا اسفه عباره عن دبل ست دي ان ايه سنجل سيركلر سوبر كويس زي الرسمه دي بالظبط عامل زي الدوده كده والسوبر كويز على بعضه ملفلف على بعضه وهو دبل استرندد وايه وسركل طيب بيدخل فيجن بتاع البكتيريا والابليكيشن وخلاص هي البكتيريا اساسا الابلكيشن بتاع هل في نوع من انواع ايه موجود في البكتيريا اخر يس اللي هي الايه اكسترا كروموسوم ايه اللي هو البلس هنعرف عنه شغلته بالتفصيل كمان شويه ده عباره عن ايه حاجه مهمه في البكتيريا فهنتكلم عليها شويه سيركلر برده زيه زي الكروموزون بس اكسترا كروموسوما ايه موجود في السيتوبلازم لوحده وعنده قدره

عجيبه سبحان الله ان هو لوحده يعني البكتيريا زيت هو لوحده يعني ممكن البكتيريا دي لسه ما عملتش اثنين اللي جوه ده بقت اتنين واربعه وتمانيه فاهمين ازاي يعني لوحده عنده جينز ابليكيشن لوحده وبيحمل جينز ودي الحاجه اللي تهمنا بيحمل جينز ده كتير يا الفيرلس مش بيحمل جينز اخرى والله انت لو بكتيري عندك ممكن ابقى شايل علي طاقسم برودكشن لا ده انا ممكن ابقى شايل على سطح البلازميد جين 4 ودي الاهميه بقى والاهميه الاكثر اللي هناخدها في محاضره البكتيريا الجيناتكس ان البلازما ده عنده القدره مش بس انه خليه واحده لان عنده القدره ان انا بكتيري نمبر وان اتنقل من بكتيريا نمبر وان نمبر 2 اختي والبلازما ده يتنقل من هنا لهنا فبدل ما بقت البكتيريا اللي عندها طاقسم بقت واحده اللي جنبها اختها بقت كمان عندها الطقس فدي اهميه البلازميد في ايه في البكتير طيب نراجع الكلام ده بقى في بتاع البكتيريا اتفقنا ان الانفلوب خلصنا بتاعه في التيبل اللي فات ان السلول بيختلف جرام ناكد لكن نيجي بقى على الاخرى من اول الكبسول للبلاي من فلاجل للكورلازم والبلازميد موجوده في جرام بلس ومش شرط مش حاجات يعني موجوده في البكتيريا في الجرام لكن الكبسول ممكن يبقى موجود اه او لا في والجرام كذلك طبعا موجود النيوكليوس او النيوكيويد او الكروموزون موجود طبعا دي موجوده مش موجوده طيب يعني ايه بكتيريا سبورز بالعربي يعني البكتيريا المتحوصله دي عباره

فلازم ابقى متاكد مش موجوده لما اجي انظف السرير ولا الاوضه بتاعه المريض لازم ابقى عارف ان الحاجات دي حواليا فلازم اعقم بطريقه سليمه وهناخد مينس ومين الحاجات اللي لازم استخدمها دي بقى اللي تهمني اكلينيكين لازم ابقى فاهم كمان ان السبورز دي هتضايقني في الترييت كمان بالانتباهوتك لان اكيد اكيد طالما هي كده يبقى هي كمان لما اجي اعرض لانسي وهو عنده وان اب مايك اللي بتكون يبقى لن يستجيب للايه للانتيباتكس فدي الاهميه ان انا اخد يعني ايه بكتيريا طيب هي بقى على المستوى البيزك هي ليه بقت سبور او ايه اللي بيخليها كده ان هي بتبقى عندها زي ما قلنا في اول السلايم اللي هي دي هايدريتد ما عندهاش ميه كتير جوه الخليه بتاعتها لان عندها ماده بتساعدها على الكلام ده اسمها كالسيوم ديفيكولونيت الكالسيوم ديكورنيت ده ماده بتخلي من البكتيريا تبقى ناشفه وتكون السبور ده طيب هل في انواع معينه من الانفكشنز انا بتعرض لها وبتخليني بيحصل لي العدوى بالسبورس المفاجاه بقى انه اه زي مين زي الانترنت يعني ايه انتركس الجمره الخبيثه الجمره الخبيثه دي من الحاجات اللي بتستخدم دلوقتي في الحروب البيولوجيه لان ميكروب ممكن اعمل به انفكشن ونهايته دس طب ليه ما استخدموش الجمره الخبيثه دي لما ناخدها في مكانها بقى هنعرف هو بيعمل ايه وعلى فكره دي حصلت قبل كده في اظن في بدايه الالفينات كان حصل او بريك في امريكا ان الناس اللي شغالين في
